nationalAnthem: High We Exalt Thee, Realm of the Free
motto: Unity, Freedom, Justice
highestPoint: Mount Bintumani / Loma Mansa (1,945 m in the Loma Mountains)
longestRiver: Rokel River (Seli River, 386 km) / Moa River / Sewa River
climate: Tropical monsoon with torrential rainfall from May to November (one of the wettest regions in West Africa, exceeding 3,000 mm annually) and a dry Harmattan season from December to April
naturalHazards: Torrential rainfall causing deadly mudslides and urban flash floods in Freetown
Harmattan winter dust storms
environmentalIssues: Deforestation on Freetown peninsula hillsides
Artisanal diamond mining siltation and water pollution
Overfishing by illegal trawlers
biodiversity: Outamba-Kilimi National Park (pristine savanna-woodland harboring chimpanzees, bongo antelopes, and pygmy hippos), Tiwai Island Wildlife Sanctuary (highest concentration of primates in West Africa), and Tacugama Chimpanzee Sanctuary
languages: English (official language of government and education)
Krio (English-based creole, universal national lingua franca spoken by >95%)
headOfGovernment: President Julius Maada Bio (Chief Minister David Moinina Sengeh)
legislature: Parliament of Sierra Leone
latestElections: General election June 2023 (Julius Maada Bio re-elected president); national unity agreement brokered with opposition; next scheduled 2028
politicalSituation: President Julius Maada Bio second term; implementation of the 'Big Five Game Changers' agenda prioritizing agricultural self-sufficiency (Feed Salone), human capital development (Free Quality Education), youth employment, infrastructure, and public service reform.
foreignRelations: Member of ECOWAS, Mano River Union, Commonwealth, OIC, African Union, UN; served as an elected member of the UN Security Council for the 2024–2025 term.
military: Republic of Sierra Leone Armed Forces (RSLAF).
adminDivisions: 4 provinces (Northern, North Western, Southern, Eastern) and the Western Area (including Freetown)
history: Inhabited by indigenous Mende, Temne, Limba, and Sherbro peoples. Portuguese explorer Pedro de Sintra arrived in 1462, naming the mountainous peninsula 'Serra Leoa' (Lioness Mountains). Bunce Island became a prominent slave trading fortress in the 18th century, from which thousands were transported to the rice plantations of South Carolina and Georgia (giving rise to the Gullah Geechee culture). In 1787, British abolitionists founded Freetown as a haven for liberated slaves ('Black Poor', Nova Scotian settlers, and Maroons), who created the Krio culture and language. Gained independence in 1961 under Sir Milton Margai. Suffered a devastating 11-year civil war (1991–2002) fueled by illicit 'blood diamonds' until peace was restored with UN and British assistance. Demonstrated remarkable resilience overcoming the 2014-2015 Ebola epidemic.
recentEvents2020_2026: Served with distinction on the UN Security Council (2024–2025); inaugurated the modern Freetown International Airport terminal at Lungi in 2023; launched the flagship 'Feed Salone' food sovereignty drive; expanded renewable hydro and solar mini-grids across rural chiefdoms.
historicalFigures: Sengbe Pieh / Joseph Cinqué (leader of the 1839 Amistad slave ship revolt)
Bai Bureh (hero of the 1898 Hut Tax War)
ethnicGroups: Krio ~2.0% (disproportionately influential in education and law)
education: Fourah Bay College (founded 1827, the oldest university college in Sub-Saharan Africa, earning Sierra Leone the historic title 'Athens of West Africa'); Njala University; Free Quality School Education (FQSE) initiative covering over 2 million students.
healthcare: Connaught Hospital and Princess Christian Maternity Hospital in Freetown; nationwide maternal and child free healthcare policy.
socialCustoms: Deep tradition of interfaith family harmony (Muslims and Christians celebrating holidays together), afternoon storytelling, lively beach football on Lumley Beach.
etiquette: Greetings with a warm handshake and inquiry about family ('How di bodi? - Di bodi fayn'), presenting items with the right hand, addressing community chiefs respectfully.
nationalIdentity: Defined by the heritage of Freetown's liberation history, the ancient Cotton Tree memory, the universally unifying Krio language, exceptional interfaith peace, and pristine Atlantic beaches.
industries: Diamond mining (alluvial and kimberlite: Koidu mine)
Rutile and ilmenite mining (Sierra Rutile: world's largest high-grade natural rutile deposit)
Bauxite mining (Vimetco)
Iron ore extraction (Marampa mine)
Artisanal and commercial fisheries
Brewing (Sierra Leone Brewery / Star Beer)
energy: Bumbuna Hydroelectric Plant (50 MW) on the Seli River and cross-border CLSG transmission line connecting to the West African Power Pool
tourism: Unspoiled natural and heritage tourism: world-class white sand beaches of the Freetown Peninsula (River Number Two Beach, Bureh Beach, Tokeh), Bunce Island slave castle heritage tours, chimpanzee tracking at Tacugama, and surfing at Bureh.
employment: Subsistence smallholder farming, artisanal diamond and gold mining, petty retail commerce in Freetown, fishing.
debtInflation: Macroeconomic restructuring supported by IMF Extended Credit Facility; transition to redenominated New Leone.
transport: Freetown modern international airport terminal connected to the capital via high-speed water taxis; Queen Elizabeth II Quay (deepwater container port).
ports: Port of Freetown (Queen Elizabeth II Quay, one of the world's largest natural harbors)
Port of Nitti (rutile and bauxite terminal)
Pepel (iron ore port)
cuisine: Cassava Leaf Soup (pounded cassava leaves cooked with smoked fish, beef, peanut paste, and red palm oil, served over white rice), Plasas (stewed greens with dried fish and chili), Groundnut Stew (savory peanut stew with chicken), Jollof Rice (Sierra Leonean style), Fry-Fry (street food: fried plantains, sweet potatoes, and fish with spicy onion-pepper sauce), Krin-Krin greens, Ginger beer with cloves.
festivals: Boxing Day street masquerades (Paddle, Hunting society masks in Freetown)
music: Palm-wine music (Maringa acoustic guitar style popularized by S.E. Rogie), Milo Jazz, Bubu music (fast spiritual processional horn music popularized by Janka Nabay), contemporary Afro-pop and hip-hop (Emmerson, Drizilik).
dance: Bubu dance, masked ancestral society dances (Mende Sowei mask dances, Hunting society masquerade).
art: Mende Sande society Sowei helmet masks (uniquely carved and worn exclusively by women, featuring high forehead and ringed neck symbolizing feminine beauty and spiritual wisdom), Nomoli soapstone ancient carvings.
architecture: Krio Board Houses (charming two-story Victorian-style wooden gingerbread houses built by liberated settlers in Freetown); historic stone churches (St. John's Maroon Church built 1820).
literature: Syl Cheney-Coker (The Last Harmattan of Alusine Dunbar), Aminatta Forna (The Memory of Love), Ishmael Beah (A Long Way Gone: Memoirs of a Boy Soldier).
cinema: Emerging independent cinema; Sierra Leone International Film Festival.
sports: Football: Leone Stars (heroic performances at the Africa Cup of Nations; global icons Mohamed Kallon, Kei Kamara), Athletics, Cricket, Surfing.
media: Awoko, Concord Times, Standard Times, SLBC (Sierra Leone Broadcasting Corporation), AYV (African Young Voices).
clothing: Traditional Gara hand-dyed tie-dye and batik fabrics; Krio formal attire; casual beachwear.
crafts: Gara tie-dyed fabrics, Mende Sowei carved masks, handwoven country cloth, cane furniture.
worldHeritageSites: Bunce Island (historic slave fortress, Tentative List)
unescoIntangible: Oral traditions of Krio storytelling and Bubu music
famousPeople: David Moinina Sengeh (global education innovator and Chief Minister)
flagDescription: Three equal horizontal bands of light green (agriculture, natural resources, and mountains), white (unity and justice), and light blue (the natural harbor of Freetown and hope for peace).
coatOfArmsDescription: Features a shield showing a lion passant beneath a serrated border (symbolizing the Lion Mountains) and three torches of education, supported by two rearing lions flanked by palm trees, over the motto 'Unity, Freedom, Justice'.
landmarks: River Number Two Beach (breathtaking white sand paradise)
Queen Elizabeth II Quay (Freetown natural harbor)

name: Somalia
nativeName: Jamhuuriyadda Federaalka Soomaaliya / جمهورية الصومال الفيدرالية
motto: None official
highestPoint: Shimbiris in the Cal Madow range (2,450 m)
longestRiver: Jubba River (1,800 km) and Shebelle River (1,500 km, vital southern agricultural basin)
majorLakes: No major permanent inland natural lakes; extensive riverine wetlands along lower Jubba-Shebelle delta
climate: Arid to semi-arid tropical desert and scrubland with year-round high temperatures; monsoon trade winds bring two rainy seasons: Gu (April–June) and Deyr (October–December)
naturalHazards: Recurring severe multi-year droughts causing livestock loss
Severe flash floods along the Shebelle and Jubba river valleys during intense El Niño rainfall
Dust storms
environmentalIssues: Deforestation for charcoal export causing desertification
Overgrazing of arid pastures
Illegal foreign fishing in territorial waters
biodiversity: Cal Madow montane cloud forests (home to the Somali wild ass, beira antelope, speke's gazelle), frankincense (Boswellia sacra) and myrrh trees, and rich coral reefs along the Gulf of Aden
languages: Somali (official and national language spoken universally across all clans)
English (widely used in business and higher education)
currency: Somali Shilling (SOS, Sh.So.) and US Dollar (ubiquitous digital mobile money: EVC Plus, Zaad, Sahal)
legislature: Federal Parliament (House of the People and Senate)
constitution: 2012 (Provisional Constitution, comprehensive constitutional review amendments enacted in 2024)
mainPoliticalParties: Wadani and Kulmiye (in Somaliland regional context)
latestElections: Presidential election May 2022 (Hassan Sheikh Mohamud elected to historic second non-consecutive term); local direct elections held in Puntland; national universal suffrage transition planned for 2026
politicalSituation: Transformative institutional recovery under President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud; joined the East African Community (EAC) in 2024; achieved complete debt cancellation under the IMF/World Bank HIPC Initiative ($4.5 billion forgiven); lifted the 30-year UN arms embargo; successfully reclaiming territory from insurgent groups with ATMIS support.
foreignRelations: Member of East African Community (joined March 2024), Arab League, African Union, OIC, IGAD, UN; strategic diplomatic partnerships with Turkey, the United States, Qatar, UAE, and EU; ongoing constitutional dialogue regarding the status of northern regions including Somaliland.
military: Somali National Army (SNA) comprising Land Forces, Navy, and Air Force.
adminDivisions: Federal structure comprising Benadir Regional Administration (Mogadishu) and Federal Member States: Galmudug, Hirshabelle, Jubaland, South West, Puntland (and northern Somaliland region)
history: Ancient Land of Punt known to Egyptian Pharaohs as the 'Land of the Gods' for its frankincense, myrrh, and aromatic resins. Medieval Somali maritime sultanates flourished: the Sultanate of Mogadishu, Ajuran Empire (renowned for hydraulic engineering and stone fortifications), Sultanate of Ifat, and Adal Sultanate led by Ahmad ibn Ibrahim al-Ghazi. Partitioned in the late 19th century into British Somaliland and Italian Somaliland. Anti-colonial Dervish state led by Sayyid Mohammed Abdullah Hassan ('Mad Mullah') resisted British forces for 20 years (1900–1920). Gained independence and unified on July 1, 1960. General Siad Barre seized power in 1969, leading to the 1977 Ogaden War and the regime's collapse in 1991. Following two decades of fragmentation, the Federal Government was established in 2012, ushering in an era of national rebirth, economic modernization, and global re-engagement.
recentEvents2020_2026: Formally admitted as the 8th member of the East African Community (EAC) in 2024; completed the IMF/World Bank HIPC debt relief process wiping out over $4.5 billion in sovereign debt; UN Security Council unanimously lifted the 31-year arms embargo; commenced offshore oil and gas exploration concessions with Turkish Petroleum; completed the first phase of constitutional modernization.
historicalFigures: Sayyid Mohammed Abdullah Hassan (Dervish leader and master poet)
Mo Farah (4-time Olympic Champion distance runner)
ethnicGroups: Somali ~85% (divided into traditional clan families: Hawiye, Darod, Isaaq, Rahanweyn/Digil-Mirifle, Dir)
Somali Bantu, Bajuni, and Benadiri minorities ~15%
education: Somali National University (reopened and expanding in Mogadishu); Mogadishu University; SIMAD University; Amoud University (Borama).
healthcare: Erdogan Hospital (Digfeer) in Mogadishu; Banadir Maternity Hospital; expanding primary health units funded by international partnerships.
socialCustoms: Xeer (traditional customary oral legal consensus system mediated by clan elders), nomadic camel pastoralism culture, afternoon tea and halwa gatherings, passionate oral poetry recitations.
etiquette: Islamic greetings (As-salamu alaykum), handshakes among same gender, right-hand use for dining and business, immense respect for family and poetic orators.
nationalIdentity: Celebrated as the 'Nation of Poets', united by a single universal language (Af-Soomaali), Islamic faith, camel pastoralism heritage, maritime seafaring, and boundless entrepreneurial vitality.
industries: World-leading digital mobile money and fintech (over 90% of transactions cashless via EVC Plus, Zaad)
Livestock export logistics (world's top exporter of live camels and sheep to Gulf states)
Telecommunications and internet service providers (Hormuud, Telesom)
Money transfer and remittance banking (Dahabshiil)
Offshore marine fisheries and seafood processing
Frankincense and myrrh harvesting and distillation
agriculture: Live animals (camels, sheep, goats, cattle - accounts for >70% of export earnings)
naturalResources: Untapped offshore crude petroleum and natural gas (estimated over 30 billion barrels)

latestElections: Watershed general election May 29, 2024 (ANC lost its absolute majority for the first time in 30 years, leading to a historic multi-party Government of National Unity led by Cyril Ramaphosa); next scheduled 2029
politicalSituation: Pivotal new political era under the multi-party Government of National Unity (GNU); successfully ended severe electrical load shedding in 2024 through Eskom turnaround and private solar/wind boom; assumed the G20 Presidency in 2025 (first African nation to chair the G20).
foreignRelations: Africa's sole G20 member and G20 President in 2025; founding member of BRICS; member of AU, SADC, Commonwealth, SACU, UN; led the landmark historic genocide case at the International Court of Justice (ICJ) in 2024; moral leader of the Global South.
military: South African National Defence Force (SANDF).
adminDivisions: 9 provinces (Gauteng, Western Cape, KwaZulu-Natal, Eastern Cape, Free State, Limpopo, Mpumalanga, North West, Northern Cape)
history: Inhabited by indigenous San and Khoekhoe peoples for tens of thousands of years, followed by Bantu migrations (Nguni and Sotho-Tswana). Jan van Riebeeck established a Dutch East India Company (VOC) victualing station at the Cape of Good Hope in 1652. British seized the Cape in 1806, prompting the Boers' Great Trek into the interior. King Shaka built the formidable Zulu Empire in the 1820s. Discoveries of diamonds at Kimberley (1867) and gold on the Witwatersrand (1886) triggered intense industrialization, the Anglo-Boer War (1899–1902), and the Union of South Africa in 1910. In 1948, the National Party enacted the brutal system of Apartheid (institutionalized racial segregation). Heroic resistance led by the African National Congress (ANC), Nelson Mandela, Walter Sisulu, Oliver Tambo, Desmond Tutu, and the 1976 Soweto Uprising eventually dismantled the regime. Nelson Mandela was released in 1990 after 27 years in prison, and the historic first democratic non-racial elections were held on April 27, 1994, inaugurating the 'Rainbow Nation'.
recentEvents2020_2026: Formed the historic Government of National Unity (GNU) following the May 2024 elections; assumed the G20 Presidency for 2025; eliminated load shedding rolling blackouts through massive private solar rollout (>6,000 MW rooftop solar installed); won back-to-back Rugby World Cup titles (2019, 2023: Springboks record 4-time champions); led landmark global ICJ cases; hosted the historic 2023 BRICS Summit expanding the bloc.

religions: Christianity (Zionist Christian, Pentecostal, Methodist, Catholic, Dutch Reformed) ~86.0%

majorLakes: The Sudd (world's largest freshwater swamp and wetland system, covering up to 90,000 km² during seasonal floods)
climate: Tropical wet-and-dry with heavy seasonal rains from May to October; hot, dry season from November to April; lush equatorial greenery in the southern Green Belt
naturalHazards: Massive perennial seasonal flooding of the Nile inundating the Sudd wetland basin
Severe droughts in southeastern and northern border rangelands

Deforestation for charcoal

languages: English (official language of government, education, and courts)
Juba Arabic (universal spoken urban lingua franca)
headOfGovernment: President Salva Kiir Mayardit (First Vice President Riek Machar)
legislature: Revitalised Transitional National Legislative Assembly (R-TNLA) and Council of States
latestElections: Independence referendum January 2011 (98.83% voted for independence); general elections scheduled under the extended peace roadmap
politicalSituation: Implementation of the Revitalised Agreement on the Resolution of the Conflict in South Sudan (R-ARCSS); power-sharing transitional government focused on security sector unification, economic diversification, and constitutional drafting.
foreignRelations: The world's newest internationally recognized sovereign nation (joined UN in July 2011); member of East African Community (EAC), African Union, IGAD, UN; close regional cooperation with Kenya, Uganda, Ethiopia, and Sudan.
military: South Sudan People's Defence Forces (SSPDF).
adminDivisions: 10 states and 3 administrative areas (Abyei, Greater Pibor, Ruweng)
history: Inhabited by Nilotic pastoralists (Dinka, Nuer, Shilluk) and Central Sudanic agriculturalists for millennia; the Shilluk Kingdom flourished from the 15th century under the Reth (divine king). Resisted slave raiding and Egyptian-Ottoman expansion in the 19th century. Incorporated into the Anglo-Egyptian Condominium of Sudan (1899–1956). Following Sudan's independence in 1956, southern grievances over political marginalization and religious Arabization sparked two protracted civil wars: the First Sudanese Civil War (Anyanya, 1955–1972) and the Second Sudanese Civil War led by John Garang's Sudan People's Liberation Movement/Army (SPLM/SPLA, 1983–2005). The 2005 Comprehensive Peace Agreement (CPA) paved the way for a historic self-determination referendum. On July 9, 2011, South Sudan officially declared independence as the 54th African state and 193rd UN member.
recentEvents2020_2026: Made global conservation history in 2024 when comprehensive aerial surveys confirmed the Great Nile Migration in Boma-Bandingilo as the world's largest land mammal migration (6 million antelopes); celebrated historic Olympic basketball triumph at the Paris 2024 Games as the Bright Stars stunned Puerto Rico and pushed Team USA; managed cross-border oil flow disruptions and refugee influx from the Sudan conflict.
historicalFigures: Dr. John Garang de Mabior (Founding father of the liberation struggle)
Luol Deng (NBA star & architect of South Sudanese basketball miracle)
education: University of Juba; Upper Nile University (Malakal); Catholic University of South Sudan; nationwide programs expanding English-curriculum primary schooling.
healthcare: Juba Teaching Hospital; Al-Sabah Children's Hospital in Juba; widespread reliance on international humanitarian healthcare partners (MSF, ICRC).
socialCustoms: Cattle culture (cattle are the foundation of wealth, social prestige, dowry / bride price, and identity among pastoralists), evening dance gatherings, wrestling matches, respect for clan elders and spiritual leaders.
etiquette: Greetings with a warm handshake and right hand cupping the elbow, asking after the welfare of family and cattle herds, gentle demeanor.
nationalIdentity: Defined by the hard-won pride of independence, the mighty White Nile and vast Sudd wetland, revered cattle keeping traditions, tall athletic stature, and basketball triumph.
industries: Crude petroleum extraction (Dar Petroleum and Greater Pioneer Operating Company in Paloch and Unity oilfields)
Brewing (South Sudan Beverages / White Bull lager)
Construction materials and quarrying
Artisanal timber and river transport
agriculture: Livestock herding (massive national cattle herd exceeding 12 million head, plus sheep and goats)
energy: Expansion of off-grid solar mini-grids (Juba Solar Project) alongside cross-border electricity interconnection plans with Uganda and Ethiopia
exports: Crude petroleum (Nile Blend and Dar Blend via pipeline to Port Sudan)
tourism: Breathtaking wilderness and safari frontier: witnessing the Great Nile Wildlife Migration in Bandingilo and Boma National Parks (world's largest mammal migration), exploring the vast Sudd swamps by boat, hiking the Imatong Mountains, and cultural encounters with traditional cattle camps.
employment: Over 75% in pastoral livestock rearing and subsistence agriculture, public administration, humanitarian sector contracting.
debtInflation: Macroeconomic stabilization supported by IMF Staff-Monitored Programs; central bank managing foreign exchange liquidity.
transport: Barge transport along the White Nile connecting Juba to Malakal and Renk; modern paved highway connecting Juba to the Ugandan border at Nimule; Juba modern river port.
airports: Juba International Airport (JUB, rapidly expanding hub)
ports: Landlocked; primary oceanic freight access through Port of Mombasa (Kenya) and Port Sudan (Sudan, crude pipeline terminal)

history: One of humanity's ancient riverine civilizational cradles: the Kingdom of Kerma (c. 2500–1500 BC) and the Kingdom of Kush. The 25th Dynasty of Egypt was founded by Kushite pharaohs (Piye, Taharqa: 'The Black Pharaohs') who conquered Egypt and built over 250 pyramids at Meroë, Karima, and Nuri—more pyramids than in all of Egypt! Converted to Coptic Christianity in the 6th century, establishing the medieval kingdoms of Nobatia, Makuria, and Alodia. Arab-Islamic expansion led to the Funj Sultanate of Sennar and the Darfur Sultanate. Conquered by Muhammad Ali Pasha of Egypt in 1821. Muhammad Ahmad proclaimed himself the Mahdi in 1881, defeating British General Charles Gordon in the Siege of Khartoum. Joint Anglo-Egyptian Condominium ruled from 1899 until independence on January 1, 1956. Led by Omar al-Bashir for 30 years (1989–2019) until ousted by a peaceful civilian popular revolution in April 2019.
recentEvents2020_2026: Mobilized humanitarian resilience and reconstruction operations centered in Port Sudan; protected ancient UNESCO archaeological sites of Meroë and Jebel Barkal; advanced gold export formalization; international peace negotiations prioritizing sovereign territorial integrity and civilian democratic transition.

history: Uninhabited volcanic islands discovered by Portuguese navigators João de Santarém and Pêro Escobar around 1470. Colonized by Portugal with enslaved Africans to pioneer large-scale sugar plantation economies. In 1595, Rei Amador led a famous slave rebellion. By the early 20th century, the islands had become the world's largest producer of cocoa ('Chocolate Islands'). Plantations (Roças) functioned as self-contained feudal villages using contract laborers (Serviçais) from Angola, Mozambique, and Cabo Verde. Gained independence on July 12, 1975 under Manuel Pinto da Costa. Transitioned to peaceful multi-party democracy in 1990 as one of Africa's earliest democratic pioneers.
recentEvents2020_2026: Príncipe celebrated over a decade as a pristine UNESCO Biosphere Reserve; expanded organic fair-trade single-estate chocolate exports (Claudio Corallo chocolate, Diogo Vaz); modernized São Tomé International Airport and Port of Fernão Dias deepwater logistics plans; expanded marine protected areas to 30% of territorial waters.

English (official, widely used in higher education, commerce, and higher courts)
government: Unitary presidential democratic republic (federation uniting Tanganyika and Zanzibar)
headOfState: President Samia Suluhu Hassan (Tanzania's first female president)
headOfGovernment: Prime Minister Kassim Majaliwa (Zanzibar President Hussein Mwinyi)
legislature: National Assembly (Bunge la Tanzania)
mainPoliticalParties: Chama Cha Mapinduzi (CCM, dominant ruling party since independence)
latestElections: General election 2020; local government elections 2024; general presidential and parliamentary elections scheduled late 2025/2026
politicalSituation: Transformative governance under President Samia Suluhu Hassan through the '4Rs' philosophy (Reconciliation, Resilience, Reforms, and Rebuilding); major opening of democratic space and press freedom; colossal infrastructure completions (Standard Gauge Railway, Julius Nyerere Hydropower Dam).
foreignRelations: Anchor of stability in East Africa; founding member of East African Community (EAC headquarters host in Arusha); member of SADC, African Union, Commonwealth, UN; historic leader of the Frontline States during the liberation of Southern Africa.
military: Tanzania People's Defence Force (TPDF).
adminDivisions: 31 regions (26 on mainland Tanganyika, 5 on Zanzibar)
history: Inhabited since the dawn of humanity (Olduvai Gorge / Oldupai, the 'Cradle of Mankind', where Mary and Louis Leakey discovered 1.75-million-year-old Zinjanthropus hominid fossils). Swahili coastal city-states (Kilwa Kisiwani, Zanzibar) dominated Indian Ocean trade in gold, spices, and ivory for centuries. Sultan of Oman moved his imperial capital to Stone Town Zanzibar in 1840. German East Africa established in 1885, met by the fierce Maji Maji Rebellion (1905–1907). Britain administered the territory after WWI as Tanganyika. Julius Nyerere ('Mwalimu' / The Teacher) led Tanganyika to peaceful independence in 1961. Following the 1964 Zanzibar Revolution led by Abeid Karume, Tanganyika and Zanzibar united on April 26, 1964, to form the United Republic of Tanzania. Nyerere championed Ujamaa (familyhood / African socialism), universal literacy, and total liberation of the African continent.
recentEvents2020_2026: Commercial launch of the modern high-speed electric Standard Gauge Railway (SGR) connecting Dar es Salaam to Morogoro and Dodoma in 2024; filled and commissioned the monumental 2,115 MW Julius Nyerere Hydroelectric Dam; advanced the $40 billion offshore LNG export project; hosted global climate and clean cooking summits under President Samia Suluhu Hassan.
historicalFigures: Mwalimu Julius Nyerere (Founding Father, Pan-African visionary)
Queen Bi Kidude (legendary Zanzibar Taarab singer)
Freddie Mercury (Farrokh Bulsara, legendary Queen lead singer born in Stone Town)
ethnicGroups: Makonde, Hehe, Maasai, Shirazi (Zanzibar), others ~69% (exemplary national cohesion without ethnic conflict)
religions: Islam (Sunni, dominant in Zanzibar ~99% and coastal areas) ~34.1%
education: University of Dar es Salaam (UDSM, historic incubator of African leaders); Sokoine University of Agriculture; Nelson Mandela African Institution of Science and Technology (Arusha); universal primary education in Kiswahili.
healthcare: Muhimbili National Hospital in Dar es Salaam; Jakaya Kikwete Cardiac Institute (premier cardiology referral center in East Africa); widespread rural dispensary networks.
socialCustoms: Deeply respectful greetings ('Shikamoo' by youths to elders, answered with 'Marahaba'), Ujamaa communal solidarity, drinking ginger-cardamom spiced tea at roadside stalls, Friday and Sunday community dress.
etiquette: Right-hand use for eating and giving items, soft-spoken courtesy, respect for traditional elders, modest attire in Zanzibar Stone Town.
nationalIdentity: Defined by the unifying power of Kiswahili, the vision of Mwalimu Julius Nyerere, Mount Kilimanjaro's snow-capped summit, the endless plains of Serengeti, and Zanzibar's fragrant spice heritage.
industries: Gold mining (Geita, Bulyanhulu, North Mara - 4th largest gold producer in Africa)
Tanzanite mining (Mirerani, world's exclusive source of the rare violet-blue gemstone)
Safari and beach tourism
Cement and construction materials
Textiles and sisal processing
Food processing and brewing (Tanzania Breweries / Kilimanjaro, Safari)
Spice processing in Zanzibar
naturalResources: Natural gas (over 57 trillion cubic feet in Songo Songo and deepwater Rovuma)
energy: Julius Nyerere Hydropower Project (2,115 MW on the Rufiji River, doubling national power capacity), Kinyerezi natural gas plants, and expanding solar mini-grids
tradePartners: India (leading buyer of gold and cashews)
tourism: World-leading wildlife and tropical beach tourism exceeding 1.8 million visitors annually: Serengeti National Park (Great Migration safaris), climbing Mount Kilimanjaro (Uhuru Peak), descending into Ngorongoro Crater, exploring UNESCO Stone Town of Zanzibar, and diving coral reefs of Mafia Island.
employment: Over 65% in agriculture and fishing, safari lodge and tour operations, mining, logistics and port services.
debtInflation: Macroeconomic stability backed by disciplined fiscal management, IMF Extended Credit Facility, and single-digit inflation.
transport: Standard Gauge Railway (SGR electric bullet trains connecting Dar es Salaam to Morogoro and Dodoma); TAZARA Railway linking to Zambia; Port of Dar es Salaam (modernized container gateway for 7 landlocked countries); fast passenger catamarans to Zanzibar.
airports: Julius Nyerere International Airport (DAR in Dar es Salaam)
Abeid Amani Karume International Airport (ZNZ on Zanzibar)
ports: Port of Dar es Salaam (primary maritime hub handling 90% of trade)
Port of Zanzibar (Malindi)
Port of Tanga
Port of Mtwara
cuisine: Ugali (stiff cornmeal porridge) served with Mchicha (braised spinach with peanut butter) and Nyama Choma (roasted goat meat), Chipsi Mayai (beloved street food: French fries cooked into an omelet, served with chili sauce and kachumbari), Zanzibar Mix / Urojo (spicy, tangy mango-tamarind broth poured over crispy chickpea fritters, potatoes, boiled egg, coconut chutney, and skewers), Pilau (fragrant spiced rice with beef, cardamom, cumin, and cinnamon), Biryani ya Zanzibar, Wali wa nazi (coconut rice), Ndizi Nyama (green cooking bananas stewed with beef).
festivals: Sauti za Busara (world-renowned African music festival in Stone Town Zanzibar every February)
Kilimanjaro Marathon (annual race at the base of Mount Kilimanjaro)
music: Bongo Flava (hugely influential modern East African Afro-pop: Diamond Platnumz, Ali Kiba, Harmonize, Zuchu), Taarab (classical Swahili coastal orchestral music popularized by Bi Kidude), Dansi (classic dance band music), Singeli (ultra-fast 200-bpm electronic street dance rhythm from Dar es Salaam).
dance: Sindimba (acrobatic Makonde dance), Mganda, Gogo dance, Chakacha.
art: Tinga Tinga painting (iconic, brightly colored, glossy enamel folk art featuring animals and village life founded by Edward Said Tingatinga), Makonde wood carvings.
architecture: Stone Town of Zanzibar (UNESCO World Heritage: coral rag stone architecture with famous intricately carved wooden brass-studded Zanzibar doors, House of Wonders, Sultan's Palace); modern high-rises in Dar es Salaam; German colonial bomas.
literature: Abdulrazak Gurnah (Nobel Prize in Literature 2021: Paradise, Afterlives, Desertion), Shafi Adam Shafi, Euphrase Kezilahabi (pioneer of modern Swahili poetry and novels).
cinema: Bongo Movie (prolific Swahili film industry in Dar es Salaam); Zanzibar International Film Festival (ZIFF).
sports: Athletics (marathon legends Filbert Bayi, Suleiman Nyambui, Alphonce Simbu World Marathon medalist), Football (Simba SC and Young Africans / Yanga: the legendary Kariakoo Derby, one of Africa's most passionate football rivalries).
media: Daily News, The Citizen, Mwananchi, TBC (Tanzania Broadcasting Corporation), Clouds Media Group, Azam TV.
clothing: Kanga (colorful cotton printed fabric featuring an inspirational Swahili proverb / Jina printed along the border, worn by women); Kitenge fabric; Kanzu white robe and Kofia embroidered cap worn by men.
crafts: Tinga Tinga canvas paintings, Makonde blackwood carvings, Zanzibar carved wooden chests and miniature doors, Maasai beaded jewelry.
worldHeritageSites: Selous Game Reserve / Nyerere National Park
Ruins of Kilwa Kisiwani and Ruins of Songo Mnara
unescoIntangible: Tradition of Tingatinga painting and Makonde woodcarving
flagDescription: A broad black diagonal band edged with yellow extending from lower hoist to upper fly, dividing the flag into a green triangle (natural vegetation and agriculture, upper hoist) and a light blue triangle (the Indian Ocean and great lakes, lower fly).
coatOfArmsDescription: Features a warrior's shield resting on Mount Kilimanjaro, supported by a man and a woman holding elephant tusks, containing a burning torch of freedom, an axe and hoe, wavy blue water, and a golden spear, with the motto 'Uhuru na Umoja'.
landmarks: Stone Town of Zanzibar (House of Wonders)
travelNotes: The ultimate safari and beach paradise; Swahili culture is extraordinarily gentle and courteous ('Karibu sana'); climbing Mount Kilimanjaro requires no technical mountaineering; Stone Town's spice-scented alleys are enchanting.
shortSummary: Tanzania is an African wonderland crowned by the snow-capped roof of the continent at Mount Kilimanjaro, the magnificent wildlife spectacle of the Serengeti migration, the exotic spice-scented UNESCO alleys of Zanzibar, and Nobel literary glory.
geography: Highest point: Mount Kilimanjaro / Kibo Peak (5,895 m, highest peak in Africa and world's highest free-standing mountain). Lowest point: Lake Tanganyika (-352 m below surface, bottom of rift lake). Longest river: Rufiji River (600 km) / Ruvuma River / Kagera River. Climate: Tropical along the coastal belt and Zanzibar with two rainy seasons (Masika from March–May, Vuli from October–December); semi-arid across central plateau; temperate in northern and southern highlands. Biodiversity: Over 38% of national territory gazetted for conservation (world-leading conservation commitment): Serengeti National Park (epicenter of the Great Migration of 1.5 million wildebeests and zebras), Ngorongoro Crater (world's largest intact volcanic caldera, home to 25,000 large animals), Selous / Nyerere National Park, and Gombe Stream (Jane Goodall's chimpanzee research site).
economy: Sectors: Services 40%, Agriculture 27%, Industry & Mining 25%, Construction 8%. Key industries: Gold mining (Geita, Bulyanhulu, North Mara - 4th largest gold producer in Africa), Tanzanite mining (Mirerani, world's exclusive source of the rare violet-blue gemstone), Safari and beach tourism, Cement and construction materials, Textiles and sisal processing, Food processing and brewing (Tanzania Breweries / Kilimanjaro, Safari), Spice processing in Zanzibar. Natural resources: Tanzanite (unique to Tanzania), Gold, Natural gas (over 57 trillion cubic feet in Songo Songo and deepwater Rovuma), Diamonds (Williamson mine at Mwadui), Nickel (Kabanga), Coal and iron ore, Hydropower and wildlife. Major exports: Gold bullion, Raw cashew nuts, Cloves, Specialty coffee, Tanzanite gemstones, Cotton, Tea.
culture: Cuisine: Ugali (stiff cornmeal porridge) served with Mchicha (braised spinach with peanut butter) and Nyama Choma (roasted goat meat), Chipsi Mayai (beloved street food: French fries cooked into an omelet, served with chili sauce and kachumbari), Zanzibar Mix / Urojo (spicy, tangy mango-tamarind broth poured over crispy chickpea fritters, potatoes, boiled egg, coconut chutney, and skewers), Pilau (fragrant spiced rice with beef, cardamom, cumin, and cinnamon), Biryani ya Zanzibar, Wali wa nazi (coconut rice), Ndizi Nyama (green cooking bananas stewed with beef).. Music & Dance: Bongo Flava (hugely influential modern East African Afro-pop: Diamond Platnumz, Ali Kiba, Harmonize, Zuchu), Taarab (classical Swahili coastal orchestral music popularized by Bi Kidude), Dansi (classic dance band music), Singeli (ultra-fast 200-bpm electronic street dance rhythm from Dar es Salaam).. Sports: Athletics (marathon legends Filbert Bayi, Suleiman Nyambui, Alphonce Simbu World Marathon medalist), Football (Simba SC and Young Africans / Yanga: the legendary Kariakoo Derby, one of Africa's most passionate football rivalries).. Festivals: Sauti za Busara (world-renowned African music festival in Stone Town Zanzibar every February), Zanzibar International Film Festival (ZIFF), Saba Saba International Trade Fair, Nane Nane Farmers Day, Kilimanjaro Marathon (annual race at the base of Mount Kilimanjaro).

name: The Gambia
motto: Progress, Peace, Prosperity
highestPoint: Red Rock (53 m, lowest national high-point in Africa)
longestRiver: Gambia River (1,120 km total course, flowing through entire country)
climate: Tropical wet-and-dry with a short, intense rainy season from June to October, and a sunny, dry season from November to May
naturalHazards: Harmattan dust winds
Riverine and coastal storm flooding
Saltwater intrusion into agricultural soils during dry season
environmentalIssues: Coastal beach erosion
Overfishing in coastal waters
Deforestation for charcoal
biodiversity: Abuko Nature Reserve and River Gambia National Park (home to chimpanzees, hippos, West African manatees, and over 540 species of migratory birds)
legislature: National Assembly
mainPoliticalParties: People's Democratic Organisation for Independence and Socialism (PDOIS)
latestElections: Presidential election 2021 (Adama Barrow re-elected); legislative elections 2022; next presidential election scheduled 2026
politicalSituation: Democratic consolidation under President Adama Barrow; hosted the 15th OIC Islamic Summit in Banjul in May 2024; implementation of the Truth, Reconciliation and Reparations Commission (TRRC) recommendations.
foreignRelations: Member of ECOWAS, Commonwealth (rejoined 2018), OIC, African Union, UN; championed the historic international case at the ICJ upholding the Genocide Convention; very close relations with Senegal (Senegambia cooperation).
military: Gambia Armed Forces (GAF) comprising Army, Navy, and National Republican Guard.
adminDivisions: 5 rural divisions and 2 municipalities (Banjul and Kanifing)
history: Part of the ancient Ghana and Mali Empires; Kaabu Empire dominated the region from the 13th to 18th centuries. Portuguese established trading posts on James Island (now Kunta Kinteh Island) in the 15th century, later sold to Britain. In 1783, Britain acquired the banks of the Gambia River, while France controlled surrounding Senegal. Gained independence in 1965 under Sir Dawda Jawara as a constitutional monarchy before becoming a republic in 1970. Yahya Jammeh seized power in a 1994 coup, ruling autocratically for 22 years until defeated in democratic elections in December 2016 by Adama Barrow.
recentEvents2020_2026: Hosted the 15th Summit of the Organization of Islamic Cooperation (OIC) in Banjul in 2024; opened the landmark Senegambia Bridge over the Gambia River; expanded modern container facilities at the Port of Banjul; achieved record European winter sun tourism.
historicalFigures: Kunta Kinteh (historic figure immortalized in Alex Haley's Roots)
Edward Francis Small (pioneer of trade unionism and self-determination)
education: University of The Gambia (UTG); American International University West Africa; expanding vocational training centers.
healthcare: Edward Francis Small Teaching Hospital (EFSTH in Banjul); network of regional clinics; pioneering Medical Research Council (MRC) unit at Fajara.
socialCustoms: Celebrated as the 'Smiling Coast of Africa' for warm hospitality (Teranga), communal Bantaba tree meeting platforms, lively naming ceremonies.
etiquette: Right-hand use for greeting and eating, inquiring warmly about health and family, respectful greetings for community elders.
nationalIdentity: Defined by the Gambia River flowing through its heart, the heritage of Kunta Kinteh, Kora harp music, Wolof and Mandinka oral praise singing (Griots / Jalolu).
industries: Tourism and coastal resort hospitality
Peanut (groundnut) shelling and oil processing
Artisanal and commercial fisheries
Port transshipment and re-export trade to Senegal/Mali
Brewing (Julbrew beer)
energy: Expansion of solar mini-grids and the 23MW Jambur solar plant, reducing reliance on heavy fuel oil generation
tourism: Premier European winter-sun holiday destination ('The Smiling Coast'): golden Atlantic beaches at Kololi and Kotu, birdwatching tours along the mangrove creeks (Bolongs), river cruises, and heritage tours to Kunta Kinteh Island.
employment: Tourism and hospitality, peanut farming smallholders, informal urban retail in Serekunda, artisanal fishing.
debtInflation: Macroeconomic stability supported by IMF Extended Credit Facility; steady Dalasi management by Central Bank of The Gambia.
transport: Senegambia Bridge at Farafenni (revolutionizing transit between northern and southern Senegal); Port of Banjul; river transport barges.
ports: Port of Banjul (deepwater river estuary port)
cuisine: Domoda (national dish: savory groundnut peanut butter stew cooked with beef or chicken and vegetables served over white rice), Benachin (one-pot Wolof seasoned rice / Jollof rice), Superkanja (okra, fish, and palm oil stew), Yassa au poulet (marinated lemon and caramelized onion chicken), Wonjo (refreshing hibiscus juice).
music: Kora (21-string harp lute pioneered by the Jobarteh, Suso, and Cissokho griot dynasties: Jaliba Kuyateh 'King of Kora', Sona Jobarteh first female professional kora master), Afro-Manding.
dance: Kanyeleng comedic dance, Lenjen Mandinka bird dance, Sabar Wolof dance.
art: Carved wooden djembe drums and koras, tie-dye and batik textile art, woven palm leaf handicrafts.
architecture: Colonial wooden and stone architecture in Banjul; Senegambian stone circles; traditional thatched riverine compounds.
literature: Ebou Dibba (Chaff on the Wind), Lenrie Peters (The Second Round, poet and surgeon), Alex Haley's Roots (ancestral setting in Juffureh).
cinema: Emerging documentary cinema; Cinekambiya International Film Festival.
sports: Traditional wrestling (Borreh, the national sport attracting huge arena crowds), Football (The Scorpions: sensational quarter-finalists at 2021 AFCON debut, 2023 AFCON appearance).
media: The Point, Foroyaa, Daily Observer, GRTS (Gambia Radio & Television Services).
clothing: Grand Boubou robes made of shining Bazin fabric with intricate embroidery; brightly colored headscarves.
crafts: Handcrafted 21-string Koras, batik wall hangings, carved wooden wildlife figurines, silver filigree earrings.
worldHeritageSites: Kunta Kinteh Island and Related Sites (including Fort Bullen and San Domingo)
Stone Circles of Senegambia (shared with Senegal)
flagDescription: Three equal horizontal bands of red (sun and savanna) and green (agriculture and forests), separated by a central blue band (Gambia River) edged with thin white stripes (peace and unity).
coatOfArmsDescription: Features an axe and a hoe crossed on a blue-and-white shield, supported by two lions (one holding an axe, one holding a hoe), topped by a heraldic helmet and oil palm over the motto 'Progress, Peace, Prosperity'.
landmarks: Kunta Kinteh Island (historic slave trade site in Juffureh)
travelNotes: Extremely welcoming and friendly destination ('The Smiling Coast'); English widely spoken; incredible haven for birdwatchers and beachgoers.
shortSummary: The Gambia, affectionately known as the 'Smiling Coast of Africa', winds along the banks of the Gambia River, celebrated worldwide as the ancestral setting of Roots, the home of enchanting 21-string Kora music, and sun-kissed Atlantic beaches.
geography: Highest point: Red Rock (53 m, lowest national high-point in Africa). Lowest point: Atlantic Ocean (0 m). Longest river: Gambia River (1,120 km total course, flowing through entire country). Climate: Tropical wet-and-dry with a short, intense rainy season from June to October, and a sunny, dry season from November to May. Biodiversity: Abuko Nature Reserve and River Gambia National Park (home to chimpanzees, hippos, West African manatees, and over 540 species of migratory birds).
economy: Sectors: Services & Tourism 65%, Agriculture 20%, Industry 15%. Key industries: Tourism and coastal resort hospitality, Peanut (groundnut) shelling and oil processing, Artisanal and commercial fisheries, Port transshipment and re-export trade to Senegal/Mali, Brewing (Julbrew beer). Natural resources: Fish and marine fisheries, Arable riverine soil, Titanium and ilmenite sand deposits, Sun, sand, and eco-tourism waterways. Major exports: Peanut products (groundnut oil and meal), Cashew nuts, Fish and seafood, Re-exports of consumer goods, Scrap metal.
culture: Cuisine: Domoda (national dish: savory groundnut peanut butter stew cooked with beef or chicken and vegetables served over white rice), Benachin (one-pot Wolof seasoned rice / Jollof rice), Superkanja (okra, fish, and palm oil stew), Yassa au poulet (marinated lemon and caramelized onion chicken), Wonjo (refreshing hibiscus juice).. Music & Dance: Kora (21-string harp lute pioneered by the Jobarteh, Suso, and Cissokho griot dynasties: Jaliba Kuyateh 'King of Kora', Sona Jobarteh first female professional kora master), Afro-Manding.. Sports: Traditional wrestling (Borreh, the national sport attracting huge arena crowds), Football (The Scorpions: sensational quarter-finalists at 2021 AFCON debut, 2023 AFCON appearance).. Festivals: Independence Day (February 18), Roots International Homecoming Festival, Banjul Cultural Festival, Tobaski (Eid al-Adha).

name: Togo
nationalAnthem: Terre de nos aïeux (Land of Our Forefathers)
motto: Travail, Liberté, Patrie (Work, Liberty, Homeland)
highestPoint: Mont Agou (986 m in the Togo Mountains)
lowestPoint: Bight of Benin / Atlantic Ocean (0 m)
longestRiver: Mono River (400 km, border river with Benin) / Oti River
majorLakes: Lake Togo (brackish lagoon in the south)
climate: Tropical hot and humid in the south with two rainy seasons (April–June, September–October); semi-arid tropical savanna in the north with a single summer monsoon and dry winter Harmattan
naturalHazards: Harmattan dusty winds
Coastal beach erosion along the Gulf of Guinea
Periodic northern droughts
environmentalIssues: Coastal zone erosion
Deforestation for fuelwood
Phosphates processing runoff
biodiversity: Fazao-Malfakassa National Park (protecting savanna elephants and antelopes in the Togo Mountains) and the sacred groves of Kpalimé
languages: French (official language of government, education, and commerce)
Ewe (national language widely spoken in south)
Kabiye (national language widely spoken in north)
government: Parliamentary republic (transitioned from presidential to parliamentary system under the new 2024 Constitution)
headOfState: President of the Republic (ceremonial head post-2024 constitution)
headOfGovernment: President of the Council of Ministers (executive head: Faure Gnassingbé)
legislature: Parliament (National Assembly and Senate)
constitution: 1992 (Fifth Republic Constitution adopted by Parliament in May 2024 establishing a parliamentary system)
mainPoliticalParties: Dynamic for the Majority of the People (DMP)
latestElections: Legislative and regional elections April 2024 (UNIR swept 108 of 113 seats); transition to the new parliamentary Fifth Republic completed in 2024
politicalSituation: Adoption of the 2024 Fifth Republic Constitution creating the executive post of President of the Council of Ministers; expansion of the Autonomous Port of Lomé as West Africa's leading container transshipment hub; Togo joined the Commonwealth of Nations in 2022.
foreignRelations: Member of ECOWAS, UEMOA, Commonwealth of Nations (joined 2022), African Union, Francophonie, OIC, UN; prominent regional mediator in Sahelian and West African diplomatic crises.
military: Togolese Armed Forces (FAT).
adminDivisions: 5 administrative regions (Maritime, Plateaux, Centrale, Kara, Savanes)
history: Inhabited by diverse indigenous peoples; ancient ironworking cultures in Bassar date back to the 5th century BC. Ewe people migrated from Oyo in the 14th century, establishing coastal chiefdoms. German explorer Gustav Nachtigal signed a treaty in 1884 with King Mlapa III at Togoville, creating the German protectorate of Togoland (the 'Model Colony' of the German Empire). Partitioned following WWI into British Togoland (which later voted to join Ghana) and French Togoland. Gained independence in 1960 under Sylvanus Olympio, who was assassinated in a 1963 military coup. Gnassingbé Eyadéma seized power in 1967, ruling for 38 years as Africa's longest-serving head of state until his death in 2005, succeeded by his son Faure Gnassingbé.
recentEvents2020_2026: Enacted the historic Fifth Republic parliamentary constitution in 2024; solidified the Autonomous Port of Lomé as the #1 container port in West Africa; expanded the Adétikopé Industrial Platform (PIA) for local cotton and garment processing; joined the Commonwealth of Nations.
historicalFigures: Nana Benz (legendary female wax print merchant tycoons of Lomé)
education: University of Lomé (historic Campus de Lomé); University of Kara; international banking and business schools (Ecobank headquarters training institutes).
healthcare: Sylvanus Olympio University Hospital Center (CHU-SO in Lomé); Dogta-Lafiè private hospital; expanding universal health coverage (AMU).
socialCustoms: Nana Benz entrepreneurial legacy (the powerful women cloth merchants who dominated the West African wax print market from Lomé's Grand Marché and drove Mercedes-Benz cars), Akossiwa voodoo purification rituals, Sunday beach football.
etiquette: Right-hand use for greeting and eating, polite inquiries about family welfare, gentle respectful handshakes.
nationalIdentity: Defined by the energy of Lomé's Atlantic waterfront, the Nana Benz trading heritage, the earthen fortress architecture of Koutammakou, and high-quality phosphate and agricultural wealth.
sectors: Services & Port Logistics 48%, Agriculture 35%, Industry & Mining 17%
industries: Deepwater container transshipment and port logistics (Port of Lomé, only natural deepwater harbor in West Africa capable of handling modern mega-containerships)
Phosphate extraction and processing (SNPT at Hahotoé)
Cement and clinker manufacturing (Cimtogo, WACEM, Scantogo)
Cotton ginning and textile garment manufacturing (PIA industrial zone)
Brewing (Brasserie du Bénin / BB Lomé, Castel)
agriculture: Cocoa and coffee (fertile Plateaux region around Kpalimé)
naturalResources: Phosphates (one of the largest deposits in Africa)
energy: Nangbéto Hydroelectric Dam on the Mono River, Kékéli Efficient Power gas plant in Lomé (65 MW), and Blitta Solar Power Plant (50 MW, one of the largest solar parks in West Africa)
tourism: Cultural and eco-tourism: visiting the UNESCO mud-tower fortress houses (Takienta) of Koutammakou, exploring the artisanal woodcarvers and butterfly rainforests of Kpalimé, the Akodessawa Fetish Market in Lomé, and relaxing along Lomé's wide palm-fringed coastal boulevards.
employment: Commerce and retail in Lomé, port handling and logistics, smallholder cotton and food crop farming, artisanal crafts.
debtInflation: Macroeconomic stability backed by UEMOA monetary discipline, euro-pegged CFA Franc, and booming port container revenues.
transport: Autonomous Port of Lomé (Lomé Container Terminal - LCT, leading transshipment hub of West Africa); modernized Lomé-Cinkassé national transit corridor linking to landlocked Burkina Faso, Niger, and Mali.
airports: Gnassingbé Eyadéma International Airport (LFW in Lomé, headquarters hub of pan-African airline ASKY)
ports: Autonomous Port of Lomé (only deepwater harbor in West Africa accommodating latest generation container vessels)
cuisine: Akumé / Pâte (stiff cornmeal or cassava dough) served with Gboma Dessi (rich spinach sauce cooked with smoked fish, beef, and crab), Fufu (pounded yams served with clear goat meat soup / Azindési peanut soup), Ablo (soft, sweet steamed fermented rice cakes), Djenkoumé (savory seasoned red corn flour cake), Ayimolou (rice and black-eyed beans cooked with sorghum leaves, served with hot chili pepper shito and fried fish), Tchoukoutou (traditional fermented sorghum beer).
festivals: Evala (famous traditional initiation wrestling festival of the Kabiye in Kara every July)
Kpessosso (Epé-Ekpé sacred stone festival of the Guen people in Glidji)
music: Highlife, Agbadza traditional drumming and dance rhythms, modern Togolese Afro-pop and gospel (King Mensah 'The Golden Voice of Togo', Toofan creators of the Ogbragada dance, Bella Bellow).
dance: Agbadza, Kamou, So dance of the Kabiye, Adjogbo royal dance.
art: Carved wooden statues and fertility figurines from Kloto, batik wall hangings from Kpalimé, woven kente-style Ewe cloth.
architecture: Koutammakou, the Land of the Batammariba (UNESCO World Heritage: remarkable two-story mud-tower fortress houses called Takienta); German colonial church at Togoville; modernist Independence Monument in Lomé.
literature: Tété-Michel Kpomassie (An African in Greenland, legendary travel memoir), Félix Couchoro, Kangni Alem (Slaves, Grand Prix Littéraire d'Afrique Noire), Kossi Efoui.
cinema: Sanneh Gordor, emerging filmmakers showcased at the Lomé International Film Festival.
sports: Canoeing / Kayak (Benjamin Boukpeti won Togo's first Olympic medal: Bronze in Slalom Kayak Beijing 2008), Football (Les Éperviers / The Sparrowhawks: historic 2006 FIFA World Cup qualification; legendary striker Emmanuel Adebayor, 2008 African Footballer of the Year and Arsenal/Real Madrid star).
media: Togo-Presse (official daily), Republicoftogo, TVT (Télévision Togolaise), Radio Lomé.
clothing: Kente-like Ewe woven ceremonial cloth; vibrant wax print fabric dresses designed by the Nana Benz; modern European casual wear.
crafts: Kpalimé carved wooden bowls and sculptures, Kloto batik textiles, woven reed baskets, ceramic pottery.
worldHeritageSites: Koutammakou, the Land of the Batammariba (remarkable mud-tower houses / Takienta, extended transboundary into Benin in 2023)
unescoIntangible: Oral heritage of Gelede and craftsmanship of Takienta earthen architecture
famousPeople: Emmanuel Adebayor (African Footballer of the Year)
flagDescription: Five equal horizontal bands of green (agricultural wealth and hope, alternating with yellow) and yellow (labor, mineral wealth, and faith), with a red square in the upper hoist canton containing a white five-pointed star (purity and peace).
coatOfArmsDescription: Features two golden lions holding bows and arrows supporting a silver shield with the letters 'RT' (République Togolaise), with two national flags, surmounted by the motto 'Travail, Liberté, Patrie'.
travelNotes: Lomé is one of West Africa's most relaxed and pleasant coastal capitals; Kpalimé offers wonderful hiking through butterfly-filled hill forests; Koutammakou is a unique architectural marvel of humanity.
shortSummary: Togo is the dynamic West African gateway of the Bight of Benin, celebrated for the UNESCO-inscribed earthen tower-fortresses of Koutammakou, the premier deepwater shipping hub of the Port of Lomé, the legendary business empire of the Nana Benz, and football icon Emmanuel Adebayor.
geography: Highest point: Mont Agou (986 m in the Togo Mountains). Lowest point: Bight of Benin / Atlantic Ocean (0 m). Longest river: Mono River (400 km, border river with Benin) / Oti River. Climate: Tropical hot and humid in the south with two rainy seasons (April–June, September–October); semi-arid tropical savanna in the north with a single summer monsoon and dry winter Harmattan. Biodiversity: Fazao-Malfakassa National Park (protecting savanna elephants and antelopes in the Togo Mountains) and the sacred groves of Kpalimé.
economy: Sectors: Services & Port Logistics 48%, Agriculture 35%, Industry & Mining 17%. Key industries: Deepwater container transshipment and port logistics (Port of Lomé, only natural deepwater harbor in West Africa capable of handling modern mega-containerships), Phosphate extraction and processing (SNPT at Hahotoé), Cement and clinker manufacturing (Cimtogo, WACEM, Scantogo), Cotton ginning and textile garment manufacturing (PIA industrial zone), Brewing (Brasserie du Bénin / BB Lomé, Castel). Natural resources: Phosphates (one of the largest deposits in Africa), Limestone and marble, Arable fertile soils, Deepwater oceanic port geography, Hydropower potential. Major exports: Refined petroleum re-exports, Natural calcium phosphates, Raw cotton, Soybeans and sesame, Clinker and cement, Cocoa and coffee.
culture: Cuisine: Akumé / Pâte (stiff cornmeal or cassava dough) served with Gboma Dessi (rich spinach sauce cooked with smoked fish, beef, and crab), Fufu (pounded yams served with clear goat meat soup / Azindési peanut soup), Ablo (soft, sweet steamed fermented rice cakes), Djenkoumé (savory seasoned red corn flour cake), Ayimolou (rice and black-eyed beans cooked with sorghum leaves, served with hot chili pepper shito and fried fish), Tchoukoutou (traditional fermented sorghum beer).. Music & Dance: Highlife, Agbadza traditional drumming and dance rhythms, modern Togolese Afro-pop and gospel (King Mensah 'The Golden Voice of Togo', Toofan creators of the Ogbragada dance, Bella Bellow).. Sports: Canoeing / Kayak (Benjamin Boukpeti won Togo's first Olympic medal: Bronze in Slalom Kayak Beijing 2008), Football (Les Éperviers / The Sparrowhawks: historic 2006 FIFA World Cup qualification; legendary striker Emmanuel Adebayor, 2008 African Footballer of the Year and Arsenal/Real Madrid star).. Festivals: Evala (famous traditional initiation wrestling festival of the Kabiye in Kara every July), Independence Day (April 27), Ayizan (bean festival in Tsévié), Kpessosso (Epé-Ekpé sacred stone festival of the Guen people in Glidji).

name: Tunisia
motto: حرية، نظام، عدالة (Freedom, Order, Justice)
highestPoint: Jebel ech Chambi (1,544 m)
lowestPoint: Chott el Djerid (-17 m endorheic salt lake)
longestRiver: Medjerda River (450 km, sole perennial river, agricultural lifeline)
majorLakes: Chott el Djerid (vast shimmering Sahara salt flat)
climate: Mediterranean along northern and coastal zones with mild rainy winters and warm dry summers; semi-arid steppe across central plains; arid to hyper-arid desert in the southern Sahara
naturalHazards: Periodic seasonal flash flooding in coastal wadis
Sirocco (hot dry Saharan wind)
Prolonged agricultural droughts
environmentalIssues: Water stress and groundwater salinization
Soil erosion and desertification in southern margins
Coastal marine conservation
biodiversity: Ichkeul National Park (vital Mediterranean wetland stopover for hundreds of thousands of migrating waterbirds, geese, and storks) and Bou-Hedma National Park
languages: French (widely used in commerce, administration, higher education)
legislature: Assembly of the Representatives of the People (ARP) and National Council of Regions and Districts
mainPoliticalParties: Parliamentary blocs supporting presidential institutional reforms; Echaâb Movement; Democratic Current; Free Destourian Party
latestElections: Presidential election October 6, 2024 (Kaïs Saïed re-elected with 90.7% of the vote); parliamentary elections 2022/2023; next presidential election scheduled 2029
politicalSituation: Consolidated presidential system under President Kaïs Saïed; implementation of the 2022 Constitution; major focus on state-led anti-corruption, public enterprise reform, agricultural food security, and green hydrogen energy exports to Europe.
foreignRelations: Member of Arab League (former headquarters host), African Union, Arab Maghreb Union, Francophonie, OIC, UN; strategic economic association agreement with the European Union (Italy, France, Germany).
military: Tunisian Armed Forces comprising Army, Navy, and Air Force.
adminDivisions: 24 governorates (wilayat)
history: Heartland of the Phoenician Carthaginian Empire founded by Queen Dido (Elyssa) in 814 BC, which rivaled Rome during the Punic Wars under legendary military genius Hannibal Barca. Conquered by Rome in 146 BC, becoming the wealthy province of Africa Proconsularis, producing monumental Roman amphitheatres (El Djem) and mosaics. Arab-Muslim expansion established Kairouan in 670 AD as the first Islamic city in North Africa, building the Great Mosque of Kairouan. Flourished under Aghlabid, Fatimid, and Hafsid Dynasties. Ottoman rule began in 1574 under the Beys of Tunis. French protectorate imposed in 1881. Independence achieved in 1956 under Habib Bourguiba, who championed women's rights (promulgating the revolutionary Code of Personal Status outlawing polygamy). Zine El Abidine Ben Ali ruled from 1987 until the historic 2010–2011 Jasmine Revolution that ignited the Arab Spring. Kaïs Saïed was elected president in 2019.
recentEvents2020_2026: Conducted the October 2024 presidential election affirming Kaïs Saïed's mandate; enacted the ELMED undersea electricity interconnector linking Tunisia to Italy; achieved record olive oil export revenues cementing position as world's #1 non-EU exporter; advanced green hydrogen transit corridors with Germany.
historicalFigures: Ibn Khaldun (Father of sociology, historiography, and modern economics, born in Tunis in 1332)
education: University of Tunis El Manar; University of Carthage; Zitouna University (one of the oldest centers of Islamic learning in the world); high proportion of female engineering and science graduates.
healthcare: Charles Nicolle Hospital and Rabta Hospital in Tunis; advanced medical infrastructure making Tunisia the leading medical tourism hub in North Africa.
socialCustoms: Café culture in seaside Sidi Bou Said and medinas, family couscous gatherings, hammam rituals, wedding jasmine bouquets (Machmoum) worn behind the ear.
etiquette: Friendly greetings with double cheek kisses among same gender, polite inquiries, removing shoes when entering traditional carpeted salons.
nationalIdentity: Defined by Carthaginian antiquity, Hannibal's courage, Ibn Khaldun's intellectual foundation, exemplary Arab-world legal rights for women, and Mediterranean aesthetic beauty.
sectors: Services & Tourism 62%, Industry & Manufacturing 28%, Agriculture & Fishing 10%
industries: Electrical wiring, automotive components, and aerospace manufacturing
Olive oil processing (world's second largest exporter of extra virgin olive oil)
Textile and high-end apparel manufacturing
Phosphate mining and chemical fertilizers (Gafsa)
Electronics and software engineering
Pharmaceutical manufacturing
Mediterranean beach and cultural tourism
agriculture: Olives and olive oil (over 100 million olive trees nationwide)
Dates (world-renowned Deglet Nour dates from Tozeur and Kebili oases)
naturalResources: Crude petroleum and natural gas (offshore Gulf of Gabès)
energy: Expansion of utility-scale solar farms (Tozeur, Tataouine) and the ELMED 600 MW undersea electrical interconnector connecting Tunisia directly to the European power grid in Sicily
tourism: Premier Mediterranean cultural and resort destination exceeding 9 million visitors annually: whitewashed blue village of Sidi Bou Said, ruins of ancient Carthage, colossal Roman Amphitheatre of El Djem, troglodyte cave dwellings of Matmata (Star Wars filming sets in Tataouine), island of Djerba, and sandy resorts of Hammamet and Sousse.
employment: Automotive and aerospace components, tourism and hospitality, agriculture and olive harvesting, civil service, IT services.
debtInflation: Macroeconomic stabilization supported by robust olive oil export windfalls, tourism recovery, and prudent policy by the Central Bank of Tunisia.
transport: Modern multi-lane toll highway network connecting Bizerte to Gabès; SNCFT passenger rail network; ELMED Mediterranean energy cable; deepwater Port of Rades and Enfidha.
ports: Port of Rades (leading container port)
Port of Bizerte
Port of Sousse
Port of Sfax
cuisine: Couscous au poisson (national dish: steamed semolina grains served with fresh Mediterranean grouper, potatoes, squash, and spiced broth), Harissa (UNESCO Intangible Cultural Heritage: spicy red chili paste blended with garlic, caraway, coriander, and olive oil, served with every meal), Brik à l'oeuf (crispy deep-fried warka pastry parcel filled with whole egg, tuna, capers, parsley, and lemon), Ojja / Shakshouka with spicy Merguez sausage, Lablabi (rich, comforting hot chickpea soup poured over torn stale crusty bread, topped with poached egg, cumin, olive oil, and harissa), Makroudh (semolina pastries stuffed with date paste, fried and dipped in honey and orange blossom syrup), Mint tea with pine nuts.
festivals: Carthage International Festival (ancient Roman amphitheatre music and theatre festival)
Carthage Film Festival (JCC, oldest African and Arab film festival)
music: Malouf (classical Arab-Andalusian orchestral music featuring oud, violin, and kanun), Mezwed (traditional bagpipe folk rhythm), modern stars like Lotfi Bouchnak, Anouar Brahem (oud jazz master), Dhafer Youssef, Emel Mathlouthi.
dance: Raqs traditional folk dance, Stambeli spiritual trance dance.
art: Roman mosaic conservation (Bardo National Museum houses the world's largest collection of Roman mosaics), painted Nabeul ceramic pottery, blue-and-white wrought iron birdcages of Sidi Bou Said.
architecture: Whitewashed Andalusian villas with brilliant cobalt blue doors and mashrabiya lattice windows in Sidi Bou Said; Roman Amphitheatre of El Djem (third largest Roman amphitheatre in the world); Great Mosque of Kairouan; ancient underground troglodyte homes in Matmata.
literature: Ibn Khaldun (The Muqaddimah), Abou el Kacem Chebbi (Will to Life: 'If a people one day wills to live, destiny must surely respond'), Mahmoud Messadi, Hélé Béji.
cinema: Férid Boughedir (Halfaouine: Boy of the Terraces), Moufida Tlatli (The Silences of the Palace), Kaouther Ben Hania (The Man Who Sold His Skin, Oscar-nominated; Four Daughters, Oscar-nominated and Cannes winner 2023); filming location for Star Wars (Luke Skywalker's home planet Tatooine named after Tataouine) and The English Patient.
sports: Tennis: Ons Jabeur ('Minister of Happiness', 3-time Grand Slam finalist: Wimbledon 2022, 2023, US Open 2022, highest-ranked African and Arab player in tennis history), Swimming: Ahmed Hafnaoui (Olympic Gold Medalist Tokyo 2020 & double World Champion) and Oussama Mellouli (2-time Olympic Gold Medalist), Football (Eagles of Carthage: 6-time World Cup participants, 2004 AFCON champions; Espérance de Tunis 4-time CAF Champions League winners).
media: La Presse de Tunisie, Le Temps, Mosaique FM, Télévision Tunisienne (Wataniya 1 & 2), Nessma TV.
clothing: Chechia (traditional crimson felt cylindrical woolen cap, the national headwear crafted by master chaouachis in the souks of Tunis); Jebba (embroidered silk and wool tunic for men); Sefsari (traditional white silk veil wrap worn by women).
crafts: Handcrafted red felt Chechia hats, hand-painted ceramic pottery from Nabeul, woven kilim rugs from Kairouan, hand-blown glass, olive wood carvings.
worldHeritageSites: Punic Town of Kerkuane and its Necropolis
Djerba: Testimony to a settlement pattern in an island territory (inscribed 2023)
unescoIntangible: Harissa, knowledge, skills and culinary and social practices (inscribed 2022)
Pottery skills of the women of Sejnane
Charfia fishing in the Kerkennah Islands
flagDescription: A red field bearing in the center a white circle containing a red crescent partially encircling a red five-pointed star (closely related to the historical Ottoman flag and adopted in 1827 by Al-Husayn II ibn Mahmud, making it one of the oldest national flags in continuous use).
coatOfArmsDescription: Features a golden shield displaying a Punic galley navigating the sea (freedom), a black lion holding a sword (order), and a pair of scales (justice), with the national motto inscribed on a scroll beneath a crescent and star.
travelNotes: A Mediterranean dream destination combining Roman majesty, seaside French-Andalusian charm, and Sahara desert adventures; delicious cuisine; safe and warm hospitality; Ons Jabeur's matches are celebrated nationwide.

name: Uganda
motto: For God and My Country
highestPoint: Margherita Peak on Mount Stanley in the Rwenzori Mountains (5,109 m)
lowestPoint: Albert Nile at the South Sudan border (614 m)
longestRiver: Victoria Nile / Albert Nile (source of the Nile River at Jinja flowing north)
majorLakes: Lake Victoria (second largest freshwater lake in the world, 45% in Uganda)
majorMountains: Rwenzori Mountains (legendary snow-capped 'Mountains of the Moon')
Mount Elgon (4,321 m extinct shield volcano)
Virunga Volcanoes (Mount Muhavura, Mount Gahinga, Mount Sabyinyo)
climate: Equatorial highland with abundant year-round rainfall and two wet seasons (March–May, September–November); pleasantly warm and spring-like year-round due to high plateau elevation ('The Pearl of Africa')
naturalHazards: Localized landslides on steep slopes of Mount Elgon during heavy rains
Periodic flash flooding in low-lying river plains
environmentalIssues: Deforestation and wetland drainage for agriculture
Soil erosion in highland farming areas
Lake Victoria water hyacinth and pollution control
biodiversity: Named by Winston Churchill as 'The Pearl of Africa': Bwindi Impenetrable National Park (harboring nearly half of the world's remaining endangered mountain gorillas), Queen Elizabeth National Park (tree-climbing lions and Kazinga Channel boat safaris), and Murchison Falls National Park
languages: English (official language of government, education, and courts)
Luganda (dominant language of the central region)
legislature: Parliament of Uganda
mainPoliticalParties: National Unity Platform (NUP, led by Robert Kyagulanyi / Bobi Wine)
latestElections: General election 2021; presidential and parliamentary elections scheduled early 2026
politicalSituation: Governed by President Yoweri Museveni since 1986; major infrastructure focus on completing the East African Crude Oil Pipeline (EACOP) and Lake Albert petroleum extraction (Tilenga and Kingfisher fields), alongside regional mediation in the Great Lakes.
foreignRelations: Member of East African Community (EAC), African Union, Commonwealth, IGAD, OIC, UN; hosted the 19th Non-Aligned Movement (NAM) Summit and G77+China Summit in Kampala in January 2024; leading troop contributor to ATMIS in Somalia.
military: Uganda Peoples' Defence Forces (UPDF).
adminDivisions: 4 administrative regions divided into 135 districts and the capital city of Kampala
history: Inhabited by hunter-gatherers, then agriculturalists and pastoralists who formed powerful centralized kingdoms: the Kingdom of Buganda (ruled by the Kabaka), Bunyoro-Kitara, Ankole, Toro, and Busoga. Arab merchants arrived in the 1840s, followed by British explorers John Hanning Speke (who identified the Source of the Nile at Jinja in 1862) and Henry Morton Stanley. British established the Uganda Protectorate in 1894. Gained independence in 1962 under Prime Minister Milton Obote with Kabaka Mutesa II as ceremonial president. Idi Amin seized power in a 1971 military coup, unleashing eight years of terror, economic devastation, and the expulsion of 80,000 Ugandan Asians. Amin was ousted in 1979 by Tanzanian forces and Ugandan exiles. Following civil conflict, the National Resistance Army (NRA) led by Yoweri Museveni took power in 1986, launching decades of economic recovery.
recentEvents2020_2026: Hosted the 19th Non-Aligned Movement (NAM) Summit and South Summit in Kampala in 2024; mobilized full construction of the 1,443 km East African Crude Oil Pipeline (EACOP) linking Lake Albert oilfields to Tanzania's port of Tanga; commissioned the 600 MW Karuma Hydroelectric Dam on the Nile; celebrated Olympic and World distance running dominance (Joshua Cheptegei, Jacob Kiplimo).
religions: Christianity (Roman Catholic ~39.3%, Anglican / Church of Uganda ~32.0%, Pentecostal ~11.1%) ~84.5%
education: Makerere University in Kampala (one of Africa's most prestigious and historic academic institutions, celebrating over a century of scholarship); Kyambogo University; Mbarara University of Science and Technology; universal primary education (UPE).
healthcare: Mulago National Referral Hospital in Kampala; Uganda Heart Institute; Uganda Cancer Institute; world-renowned pioneer in overcoming HIV/AIDS through open public awareness (ABC model).
socialCustoms: Kwanjula (traditional Buganda introduction and engagement ceremony), Rolex street snack culture, communal matooke peeling, passionate enthusiasm for football and music.
etiquette: Kneeling slightly when greeting elders (among women in Buganda culture), gentle two-handed handshakes, warm inquiries after family welfare, soft-spoken manners.
nationalIdentity: Celebrated as 'The Pearl of Africa', defined by the mist-shrouded mountain gorillas of Bwindi, the Source of the Nile, glorious royal kingdom heritage, and world distance running champions.
industries: Petroleum extraction and pipeline infrastructure (Tilenga and Kingfisher Lake Albert oilfields, EACOP)
Coffee processing and roasting (top African coffee exporter)
Hydropower generation (Karuma 600 MW, Bujagali, Nalubaale)
Cement and steel manufacturing (Tororo, Roofings Group)
Beverage brewing and distilling (Nile Breweries / Nile Special, Uganda Breweries / Bell Lager)
Food processing and sugar refining (Kakira, Lugazi)
agriculture: Coffee (Robusta native to Uganda, Arabica on Mount Elgon - top coffee exporter in Africa)
Bananas / Matooke (second largest producer in the world)
naturalResources: Crude petroleum (over 6.5 billion barrels in Lake Albert basin)
energy: Abundant green clean electricity from the Nile: Karuma Hydroelectric Dam (600 MW), Bujagali Dam, and Isimba Dam generating massive surplus power exported to Kenya, Rwanda, and South Sudan
tourism: World-class primate and wildlife adventure tourism: trekking endangered mountain gorillas in Bwindi Impenetrable Forest and Mgahinga, viewing tree-climbing lions in Ishasha (Queen Elizabeth National Park), white-water rafting the rapids of the Nile at Jinja, hiking the snow-capped Rwenzori Mountains, and boat cruises to the base of Murchison Falls.
employment: Over 68% in smallholder agriculture (coffee, tea, matooke), informal commerce in Kampala, tourism and hospitality, construction.
debtInflation: Macroeconomic stability backed by Bank of Uganda independent inflation-targeting framework; stable Ugandan Shilling.
transport: Modern Entebbe-Kampala Expressway; Standard Gauge Railway (SGR) connection projects; Port Bell and Jinja lake freight links on Lake Victoria; expanded Entebbe International Airport.
airports: Entebbe International Airport (EBB, on the shores of Lake Victoria)
ports: Landlocked; primary oceanic freight access through Port of Mombasa (Kenya, via Northern Corridor) and Port of Dar es Salaam (Tanzania, via Central Corridor)
cuisine: Rolex (legendary Ugandan street food: warm rolled chapati wrapped around a freshly fried vegetable omelet with diced tomatoes, onions, and cabbage—'rolled eggs' / Rolex), Matooke (green cooking bananas steamed in banana leaves, mashed into a smooth golden mound, served with rich beef, chicken, or groundnut peanut sauce), Luwombo (royal Buganda dish: chicken, beef, or smoked fish with mushrooms and peanut sauce wrapped and slow-steamed inside banana leaves), Posho (cornmeal porridge), Malewa (smoked bamboo shoots from Mount Elgon cooked in peanut sauce), Roasted gonja (sweet plantains), Nile Special beer.
festivals: Nyege Nyege Festival (internationally celebrated 4-day electronic and traditional African music festival in Jinja)
Martyrs' Day (June 3, pilgrimage of millions to Namugongo Shrine)
music: Kadongo Kamu (traditional acoustic guitar storytelling music), modern Ugandan Afro-beat, dancehall, and R&B (Bobi Wine, Eddy Kenzo Grammy nominee and BET Award winner, Jose Chameleone, Bebe Cool, Sheebah Karungi, Vinka).
dance: Bakisimba (graceful royal Buganda court dance mimicking the swaying of banana trees and drunk royal steps), Bwola royal Acholi dance, Runyege courtship dance.
art: Barkcloth making (UNESCO Intangible Cultural Heritage: ancient craft of harvesting and beating the inner bark of the Mutuba fig tree into soft terracotta-colored cloth), woven raffia peace baskets, soapstone and wood carvings.
architecture: Kasubi Tombs (UNESCO World Heritage: monumental circular thatched royal burial palace of the Buganda Kings); Uganda Martyrs Shrine at Namugongo; colonial architecture at Makerere University.
literature: Okot p'Bitek (Song of Lawino, monumental African classic), Jennifer Nansubuga Makumbi (Kintu, The First Woman), Moses Isegawa (Abyssinian Chronicles).
cinema: Queen of Katwe (starring Lupita Nyong'o and David Oyelowo, filmed in Kampala), Wakaliwood (ultra-low-budget DIY gonzo action cinema in the slums of Wakaliga: Who Killed Captain Alex?); Uganda Film Festival.
sports: Long-distance athletics world supremacy: Joshua Cheptegei (10,000m Olympic Gold Medalist Paris 2024, 5,000m Olympic Gold Tokyo 2020, 5,000m and 10,000m World Record Holder, 3-time World Champion), Jacob Kiplimo (Half-Marathon World Record Holder & World Cross Country Champion), Peruth Chemutai (Olympic Gold 3000m Steeplechase Tokyo 2020 & Silver Paris 2024), John Akii-Bua (1972 Olympic 400m Hurdles Gold and World Record), Football (Uganda Cranes).
media: New Vision, Daily Monitor, NBS Television, NTV Uganda, Bukedde.
clothing: Gomesi / Busauti (striking formal floor-length dress with exaggerated pointed shoulders, square neckline, and a wide silk sash tied around the waist, worn by women); Kanzu white robe worn by men with a tailored suit jacket.
crafts: Barkcloth textiles, woven banana fiber and raffia baskets, carved wooden gorilla sculptures, musical instruments (Adungu arched harp).
worldHeritageSites: Tombs of Buganda Kings at Kasubi
unescoIntangible: Bigwala, gourd trumpet music and dance of the Busoga Kingdom
famousPeople: Joshua Cheptegei (Olympic Champion & World Record Holder)
flagDescription: Six equal horizontal bands of black (the African people), yellow (the bright African sunshine), and red (the brotherhood of all mankind), repeated twice, with a white disk in the center bearing a Grey Crowned Crane (the national bird, facing the hoist).
coatOfArmsDescription: Features a shield and crossed spears over the green slopes of the Rwenzori mountains and source of the Nile, supported by a Kob antelope and a Grey Crowned Crane, depicting a drum, sun, and Nile waters, above the motto 'For God and My Country'.
travelNotes: Earns its legendary title 'The Pearl of Africa' with lush green beauty, warm spring-like climate, and unmatched wildlife safaris; tracking mountain gorillas in Bwindi is life-changing; tasting a freshly made street Rolex is a national rite of passage.
