Zanabazar (First Bogd Gegeen, master sculptor and Renaissance polymath)
ethnicGroups: Zakhchin, Uriankhai, Darkhad, Tsaatan (reindeer herders), and other ethnic groups ~6.2%
education: National University of Mongolia (NUM), Mongolian University of Science and Technology (MUST), and Mongolian State University of Agriculture; universal basic education; literacy among nomadic herders supported by mobile boarding schools.
healthcare: First Central Hospital of Mongolia and National Cancer Center in Ulaanbaatar; expanding mobile medical caravans delivering healthcare across remote sums and aimags.
socialCustoms: Nomadic hospitality where the door of the Ger (yurt) is never locked and tea and food are always set out for passing travelers; greeting with a traditional silk scarf (Khadag) presented on open palms; sharing the snuff bottle (Khoorog); honoring the hearth fire.
etiquette: Never step on the threshold (Toono) of a Ger (seen as stepping on the host's neck); accept food and drink with the right hand supported at the elbow by the left hand; walk around the central Ger pillars clockwise; respect the sacred blue sky (Tenger).
nationalIdentity: Fierce pride in Genghis Khan and the historic Mongol Empire, the freedom of nomadic pastoral life, the bond with horses (the five sacred animals: horse, sheep, goat, cattle/yak, camel), and resilient democratic sovereignty between two authoritarian superpowers.
sectors: Mining & Extractive Industry 30%, Services 46%, Agriculture & Animal Husbandry 13%, Manufacturing & Construction 11%
industries: Copper and gold mining (Oyu Tolgoi - one of the world's largest high-grade copper mines, partnered with Rio Tinto)
Coking coal extraction (Tavan Tolgoi - massive coking coal deposits exported to China)
Cashmere wool processing (Gobi Cashmere - world's #2 producer of raw cashmere)
Iron ore and fluorspar mining
Molybdenum and uranium (Zuilvch Ovoo project with Orano)
Meat and dairy processing
Felt and leather goods
agriculture: Livestock pastoralism (over 70 million head of livestock: sheep, goats, cattle, horses, yaks, and two-humped Bactrian camels)
Wheat and barley cultivation in the northern Selenge basin
naturalResources: Vast world-class mineral wealth: copper, coking coal, gold, uranium, iron ore, rare earths, fluorspar, and molybdenum
Untapped wind and solar potential across the Gobi Desert
energy: Dominated by coal-fired thermal power plants in Ulaanbaatar; advancing massive wind and solar installations in the Gobi Desert to export clean power under the Asian Super Grid concept; negotiating feasibility studies for the "Power of Siberia 2" gas transit pipeline from Russia to China
exports: Coking and thermal coal (primarily transported by rail and truck to China)
Raw and processed dehaired cashmere wool
imports: Refined petroleum fuels and diesel (from Russia)
Mining machinery and heavy dump trucks
Motor vehicles (widespread use of Toyota Prius hybrids in Ulaanbaatar)

Russia (major supplier of petroleum and electricity)
tourism: Surpassed 800,000 international tourists drawn to the Naadam Festival, the pristine wilderness of Lake Khövsgöl, camel trekking in the Gobi Desert and singing dunes of Khongoryn Els, eagle hunting with Kazakh berkutchi in Bayan-Ölgii, and horse riding across the endless steppe.
employment: Over 25% of the national workforce is directly engaged in nomadic livestock husbandry; rapid employment expansion in modern open-pit and underground mining engineering, logistics, and cashmere garment design.
debtInflation: Bank of Mongolia (Mongolbank) maintains foreign exchange reserves exceeding $5 billion; currency stabilized; inflation managed around 6-7% through monetary policy adjustments.
transport: Trans-Mongolian Railway (historic branch of the Trans-Siberian line connecting Moscow to Beijing via Ulaanbaatar); newly commissioned Tavan Tolgoi-Gashuunsukhait and Zuunbayan heavy-haul mineral railways; modern Chinggis Khaan International Airport opened in 2021; Millennium Road paved highway network.
airports: Chinggis Khaan International Airport (UBN in Khöshig Valley - state-of-the-art international gateway opened in 2021)
Buyant-Ukhaa Airport (former international airport, now domestic and charter hub)
ports: Landlocked; relies on maritime transit access through China's Port of Tianjin and Russia's Port of Vladivostok
internetUsage: 84.2% (nomadic herders use solar panels, satellite dish receivers, and Starlink satellite internet across the open steppe)
cuisine: Heavy reliance on meat and dairy ("red food" in winter, "white food" in summer): Buuz (steamed dough dumplings stuffed with spiced minced mutton or beef and onions, bursting with savory broth), Khorkhog (authentic nomadic barbecue: meat and potatoes cooked inside a sealed metal milk jug with fire-heated river stones), Boodog (traditional barbecue of whole goat or marmot roasted from the inside using red-hot stones), Tsuivan (hearty stir-fried handmade noodles with mutton and vegetables), Bansh (smaller boiled meat dumplings in tea or soup), Airag (fermented mare's milk, tangy and effervescent national drink), Aaruul (dried curd cakes dried on the roof of the Ger), and Suutei Tsai (hot salted milk tea, often simmered with butter and roasted millet).
festivals: Naadam Festival (July 11–13 - "The Three Games of Men": traditional wrestling, horse racing across the open steppe by child jockeys, and archery, UNESCO Intangible Cultural Heritage)
Tsagaan Sar (White Moon / Lunar New Year celebrated with mountains of Buuz and family blessings)
Golden Eagle Festival in Bayan-Ölgii (Kazakh eagle hunters demonstrating horseback hunting skills in October)
Thousand Camel Festival in the Gobi
music: Morin Khuur (Horsehead Fiddle - sacred two-stringed national musical instrument with a carved horse head, UNESCO); Khoomei (Throat Singing / Overtone singing where a single singer produces multiple distinct harmonic notes simultaneously, UNESCO); Urtyn Duu ("Long Song" - epic melancholic melodies with astonishing vocal ornamentation and immense pitch range, UNESCO); global folk-metal sensation The HU (combining traditional Morin Khuur, Tovshuur, and throat singing with heavy rock).
dance: Biyelgee (traditional Mongolian body and shoulder dance performed in the confined space of a Ger to the music of the Morin Khuur, expressing the daily chores of nomadic life).
art: Zanabazar's exquisite gilded bronze Buddhist sculptures (the "Michelangelo of Asia"); Thangka scroll painting; Appliqué silk embroidery; intricate silver bowls (Ayaga); traditional calligraphy in vertical Mongolian script (UNESCO).
architecture: The Ger (Yurt - aerodynamic, collapsible circular dwelling constructed of wooden lattice walls / Khana, roof poles / Uni, central crown / Toono, and felt coverings, insulated for extreme winter cold); Erdene Zuu Monastery (first Buddhist monastery built on the ruins of Karakorum); Gandantegchinlen Monastery in Ulaanbaatar (housing the 26.5m golden statue of Avalokiteshvara); giant 40-meter stainless steel Equestrian Statue of Genghis Khan at Tsonjin Boldog.
literature: The Secret History of the Mongols (13th-century chronicle, foundational historical and literary epic of Genghis Khan's life and empire, UNESCO Memory of the World); classical poetry by Dulduityn Danzanravjaa; modern literature by Dashdorjiin Natsagdorj ("My Homeland").
cinema: Mongolian cinema renaissance; documentary masterpieces ("The Story of the Weeping Camel" and "The Cave of the Yellow Dog" by Byambasuren Davaa, Oscar nominated); contemporary historical epics and international co-productions.
sports: Bökh (traditional Mongolian wrestling: no weight classes, wrestlers wear the Zodog vest and Shuudag briefs, performing the eagle dance / Deveh before the match; loss occurs when any body part other than feet touches the ground); Horse Racing (endurance cross-country races of 15 to 30 km ridden by young children); Archery; Judo (Naidangiin Tüvshinbayar won Mongolia's first-ever Olympic Gold in 2008; multiple Olympic medals in 2020 & 2024); Freestyle Wrestling; Boxing; Olympic Shooting; Sumo (Mongolian rikishi have dominated Japanese professional sumo for over two decades: legendary Yokozunas Asashoryu, Hakuho, Harumafuji, Kakuryu, Terunofuji).
media: Montsame National News Agency, Mongol TV, Eagle News TV, Zuunii Medee, and prominent English portal The UB Post.
clothing: Deel (traditional ankle-length tunic with a high collar, overlapping front, and long sleeves, secured with a bright silk sash / Bus; adapted for horseback riding and extreme cold with sheepskin or silk linings); Gutal (traditional leather riding boots with upturned toes designed not to disturb the earth or damage grass); Malgai (conical fur-trimmed hat).
holidays: Tsagaan Sar (Lunar New Year, 3 days in Jan/Feb)
Genghis Khan Day / National Pride Day (first day of winter lunar month)
crafts: Traditional Ger building, Morin Khuur instrument crafting, felt rug making, silver metalwork (silver bowls and horse saddles), and leather carving.

flagDescription: Three equal vertical bands of red (hoist, symbolizing progress and prosperity), blue (middle, symbolizing the eternal blue sky), and red (fly); centered on the hoist-side red band is the golden national emblem of Mongolia, the Soyombo (an ancient geometric ideogram representing fire, sun, moon, two fish, two triangles, and two vertical bars symbolizing national freedom and sovereignty).
coatOfArmsDescription: A circular blue emblem featuring the Wind Horse (Khiimori) galloping within the Soyombo ideogram, bordered by a continuous swastika-patterned wheel of eternity, surmounted by the Three Jewels (Cintamani), backed by a lotus base and flanked by a traditional green scarf (Khadag).
landmarks: Genghis Khan Equestrian Statue at Tsonjin Boldog (giant 40m stainless steel monument)
Flaming Cliffs (Bayanzag in the Gobi Desert - where Roy Chapman Andrews discovered the first dinosaur eggs in 1923)
Khustain Nuruu National Park (wild Takhi horses)
travelNotes: Visa-free entry for citizens of over 60 countries under the "Visit Mongolia" national initiative; summer months (June to August) offer glorious sunny weather, green steppe landscapes, and the Naadam Festival; winter travel offers dramatic frozen landscapes and eagle hunting festivals but requires heavy sub-zero thermal gear; cash (Tögrög) and local cards are widely used in Ulaanbaatar, while cash is essential in rural aimags.

Climate: Extreme continental subarctic; harsh, bone-chilling winters with temperatures falling below -40°C, and short, warm summers; over 250 sunny days per year ("Land of the Eternal Blue Sky").

name: Myanmar
officialName: Republic of the Union of Myanmar
nativeName: ပြည်ထောင်စု သမ္မတ မြန်မာနိုင်ငံတော် (Pyidaunzu Thanmăda Myăma Nainngandaw)
nationalDay: January 4 (Independence Day from Britain in 1948) / National Day (celebrated in late autumn according to lunar calendar)
nationalAnthem: Kaba Ma Kyei (Till the End of the World, Myanmar)
motto: None (Unofficial)
coastline: 1,930 km (Bay of Bengal and Andaman Sea coastline, including the Mergui Archipelago)
highestPoint: Hkakabo Razi (5,881 m in northern Kachin State - highest peak in Southeast Asia)
longestRiver: Irrawaddy River (Ayeyarwady, 2,288 km total; the lifeblood of Myanmar flowing north to south into the vast Irrawaddy Delta)
majorLakes: Inle Lake (famous for leg-rowing fishermen and floating gardens)
Indawgyi Lake (largest natural lake in Southeast Asia)
Rih Dil (heart-shaped lake in Chin State)
climate: Tropical monsoon; southwest monsoon season from June to September (bringing torrential rains to coastal and delta areas), cool dry season from October to February, and hot dry season from March to May with temperatures exceeding 40°C in the central dry zone
naturalHazards: Severe tropical cyclones from the Bay of Bengal (e.g., Cyclone Nargis in 2008, Cyclone Mocha in 2023)
Earthquakes along the active Sagaing Fault line
Monsoon flooding and landslides
environmentalIssues: Deforestation of virgin teak forests
Illegal artisanal jade, gold, and rare earth mining causing environmental degradation
Mangrove loss in the Irrawaddy Delta
Freshwater siltation in Inle Lake
biodiversity: Vast biodiversity spanning Himalayan snows to tropical coral reefs: home to the Irrawaddy dolphin, Indochinese tiger, Asian elephant, red panda, sun bear, Hoolock gibbon, and green sea turtles
languages: Burmese (Bamar - official Sino-Tibetan language with unique rounded script)
government: Unitary military junta administration (State Administration Council - SAC) facing nationwide armed opposition and parallel National Unity Government (NUG)
headOfState: Acting President Myint Swe / SAC Chairman Senior General Min Aung Hlaing
headOfGovernment: Prime Minister Senior General Min Aung Hlaing
legislature: Pyidaungsu Hluttaw (Assembly of the Union - suspended following the February 2021 coup)
constitution: Enacted in 2008; drafted under military supervision guaranteeing 25% of parliamentary seats and key security ministries to the armed forces
mainPoliticalParties: Union Solidarity and Development Party (USDP - military-aligned); National League for Democracy (NLD - dissolved by junta commission in 2023; leaders Aung San Suu Kyi and Win Myint detained); National Unity Government (NUG parallel administration); ethnic political parties
latestElections: November 2020 general election (overwhelmingly won by the NLD, subsequently annulled by the military); military regime repeatedly proposed multi-party elections postponed due to state of emergency and nationwide civil war
politicalSituation: Since the military coup of February 1, 2021 that ousted the democratically elected government of Aung San Suu Kyi, Myanmar has been engulfed in a multi-front civil war. A nationwide popular resistance movement, comprising the People's Defence Forces (PDF) aligned with the National Unity Government (NUG) and long-standing Ethnic Armed Organizations (EAOs), launched coordinated offensives. The historic "Operation 1027" (launched in late 2023 by the Three Brotherhood Alliance in northern Shan State and Rakhine) captured dozens of towns, border trade crossings to China, and regional military commands, severely contracting the junta's territorial control and deepening economic distress through 2024–2026.
foreignRelations: Subject to broad Western economic, arms, and financial sanctions; maintains essential diplomatic, energy, and defense relationships with China and Russia; complex relations within ASEAN (which bars junta political representatives from high-level summits under the stalled Five-Point Consensus); commercial engagement with Thailand and India.
military: Tatmadaw (Myanmar Armed Forces: Myanmar Army, Myanmar Air Force, Myanmar Navy; facing severe manpower shortages leading to the enforcement of mandatory conscription in 2024; opposed by coalition EAOs and PDF forces).
adminDivisions: 7 regions (dominated by Bamar majority: Ayeyarwady, Bago, Magway, Mandalay, Sagaing, Tanintharyi, Yangon) and 7 ethnic states (Chin, Kachin, Kayah, Kayin, Mon, Rakhine, Shan), plus the Naypyidaw Union Territory
history: Inhabited since antiquity by Pyu city-states and Mon kingdoms, Myanmar was unified in 1044 AD by King Anawrahta, founder of the Pagan (Bagan) Empire. He embraced Theravada Buddhism, and during the next two centuries, over 10,000 Buddhist temples and stupas were constructed across the Bagan plains. Mongol invasions under Kublai Khan shattered Bagan in 1287, leading to divided regional kingdoms (Ava, Hanthawaddy Pegu, Mrauk U in Rakhine). King Bayinnaung of the Taungoo Dynasty reunified the realm in the 16th century, creating the largest empire in Southeast Asian history. The Konbaung Dynasty (1752–1885) under Alaungpaya expanded Burmese dominion before clashing with the British East India Company. Through three Anglo-Burmese Wars (1824–1885), Britain colonized Burma, incorporating it as a province of British India, culminating in the exile of the last king, Thibaw, in 1885. General Aung San negotiated independence following World War II but was tragically assassinated in July 1947 alongside six cabinet colleagues. Burma achieved independence on January 4, 1948, under Prime Minister U Nu, immediately confronting armed communist and ethnic insurgencies. In 1962, General Ne Win led a military coup, establishing the isolationist "Burmese Way to Socialism". The nationwide 1988 pro-democracy uprising (8888 Uprising) gave rise to Aung San Suu Kyi and the National League for Democracy (NLD). A brief period of political opening and quasi-civilian democratic transition occurred between 2011 and 2020, bringing rapid economic modernization before the military abruptly seized power again in February 2021.
recentEvents2020_2026: The February 2021 military coup triggered nationwide strikes (Civil Disobedience Movement - CDM) and an unprecedented armed resistance movement combining young urban pro-democracy fighters with experienced ethnic armed armies. In October 2023, the Three Brotherhood Alliance launched "Operation 1027", capturing critical northern border crossings and towns in Shan State and Rakhine. Through 2024–2026, the military junta enforced nationwide conscription, faced intense fuel shortages and inflation exceeding 30%, lost control over major frontier trade routes to China and Thailand, while Aung San Suu Kyi remained detained under administrative sentences.
historicalFigures: Aung San Suu Kyi (Nobel Peace laureate)
U Thant (third Secretary-General of the United Nations)
ethnicGroups: Kachin, Chin, Kayah, and over 100 other recognized indigenous nationalities ~5%
religions: Christianity (Baptist, Catholic - widespread in Chin, Kachin, and Karen states) ~6.2%
Islam (predominantly in Yangon and Rakhine State) ~4.3%
education: Historic universities include University of Yangon ("Rangoon University", historic cradle of student independence protests) and Mandalay University; higher education severely disrupted post-2021 by student and faculty boycotts.
healthcare: Public hospital system supplemented by private clinics; facing severe personnel shortages and strain due to civil conflict; international humanitarian agencies delivering emergency care in border conflict zones.
socialCustoms: Wearing Thanaka (fragrant golden-yellow paste ground from tree bark applied to cheeks and foreheads as natural sun protection, cooling cosmetic, and skin treatment); widespread chewing of Kun-ya (betel nut quid with slaked lime and tobacco); communal novitiation ceremonies (Shinbyu) for young boys entering the Buddhist monkhood.
etiquette: Showing deep reverence to monks and elders; touching one's right elbow with the left hand when giving or receiving money; never touching another person's head or stepping over anyone's body; removing shoes and socks completely before entering temple grounds and pagodas.
nationalIdentity: A complex tapestry of deep Theravada Buddhist devotion, sacred pagoda construction, pride in ancient royal empires (Bagan, Taungoo), and an ongoing, heroic struggle for federal democracy and ethnic self-determination.
industries: Natural gas extraction (offshore Yadana and Shwe fields supplying Thailand and China)
Jade and gemstone mining (Hpakant jade mines - world's finest imperial jade, and Mogok rubies)
Rare earth mining (Kachin State - supplying major shares of global dysprosium and terbium to China)
Garment and footwear manufacturing
Timber processing and teak harvesting
Food and rice milling
agriculture: Rice (Irrawaddy Delta is the historic "rice bowl" of Burma)
Pulses and beans (world-leading exporter of black gram and pigeon peas)
naturalResources: Offshore natural gas reserves (Gulf of Martaban)
Imperial jadeite (world's #1 producer, supplying >70% of global jade)
energy: Natural gas and hydroelectric power generate domestic electricity; substantial gas export revenues earned through pipelines to Thailand and China; chronic urban power rationing in Yangon and Mandalay post-2021
exports: Offshore natural gas (to Thailand and China via cross-border pipelines)
tradePartners: Thailand (major energy customer and consumer goods supplier)
tourism: Historically celebrated for Bagan's 2,000 ancient temples, Shwedagon Pagoda, Inle Lake, and pristine Ngapali Beach; international tourism severely curtailed by post-2021 political instability and conflict advisories.
employment: Agriculture and rural subsistence farming employ ~60% of the population; millions of Myanmar migrant workers in Thailand, Malaysia, and Singapore sending vital family remittances.
debtInflation: Severe currency depreciation of the Kyat; high consumer inflation (>30%); parallel black-market foreign exchange rates operating alongside official central bank tiers.
transport: Yangon-Mandalay Expressway and railway corridor; Irrawaddy River passenger and cargo barges; border trade corridors to Ruili (China) and Mae Sot (Thailand) frequently disrupted by armed conflict.
airports: Yangon International Airport (RGN - primary international gateway)
ports: Port of Yangon and Thilawa Special Economic Zone deepwater port; planned Kyaukphyu deepwater port (Sino-Myanmar corridor on the Bay of Bengal)
internetUsage: 44.0% (stringent internet censorship, frequent regional shutdowns in conflict zones, and high mobile data taxation enforced by the junta; pervasive use of VPNs)
cuisine: Mohinga (national dish: savory rice vermicelli in a rich, fragrant broth of minced catfish, lemongrass, ginger, garlic, toasted chickpea flour, and banana tree stems, topped with crispy fritters, boiled egg, and coriander), Laphet Thoke (world-famous fermented tea leaf salad tossed with roasted peanuts, crunchy fried yellow split peas, toasted sesame seeds, garlic chips, diced tomatoes, dried shrimp, and green chilies), Shan Noodles (sticky rice noodles in spiced tomato-chicken or pork sauce), Ohn No Khao Swè (curried chicken noodle soup in coconut milk), and Burmese curries accompanied by Ngapi Yay (fermented fish dipping sauce with fresh herbs and raw vegetables).
festivals: Thingyan (Burmese Water Festival marking the New Year in mid-April with joyous nationwide water throwing)
Thadingyut Festival (Festival of Lights in October celebrating the Buddha's descent from heaven, with millions of candles and paper lanterns)
Tazaungdaing Festival (hot-air balloon festival in Taunggyi)
music: Hsaing Waing (traditional Burmese gong and drum circle orchestra featuring the Pat Waing drum circle, Kyi Waing bronze gongs, Hne double-reed oboe, and Si bells); Saung Gauk (arched 16-stringed Burmese harp, national musical symbol of exquisite elegance); contemporary Burmese underground hip-hop and indie rock expressing anti-junta resistance.
dance: Yein (graceful synchronized ensemble dance performed by troupes of women during Thingyan); traditional Marionette theatre (Yoke thé - puppetry that historically influenced classical dance movements).
art: Pan Sel Myo (the Ten Traditional Arts: lacquerware, gold leaf pounding, bronze casting, stone carving, woodcarving, painting, stucco, blacksmithing, turnery, and silversmithing); exquisite gold leaf applied to the Mahamuni and Shwedagon statues.
architecture: Shwedagon Pagoda in Yangon (magnificent 99-meter golden pagoda encrusted with over 7,000 diamonds, rubies, and sapphires, crowned by a 76-carat diamond); the monumental brick temples of Bagan (Ananda Temple, Thatbyinnyu, Dhammayangyi); wooden monasteries (Shwenandaw Monastery in Mandalay); U Bein Bridge (world's oldest and longest teakwood bridge, 1.2 km).
literature: Classical Buddhist treatises and court poetry (Yadu); modern literature of Thakin Kodaw Hmaing; acclaimed contemporary writers like Pascal Khoo Thwe ("From the Land of Green Ghosts") and Ludu Daw Amar.
cinema: Historic cinema industry founded in 1920 (first feature "Love and Liquor"); contemporary independent cinema flourishing underground and among diaspora filmmakers documentarians capturing the post-coup struggle.
sports: Chinlone (traditional non-competitive team sport where six players pass a woven rattan ball gracefully with feet, knees, and shoulders); Lethwei (traditional Burmese bare-knuckle kickboxing, renowned as the "Art of Nine Limbs" allowing headbutts, punches, kicks, elbows, and knees); Football (passionate fan base; Aung Thu).
media: State-run outlets (MRTV, The Global New Light of Myanmar); heroic independent exiled and underground media (Democratic Voice of Burma / DVB, The Irrawaddy, Myanmar Now, Khit Thit Media).
clothing: Longyi (traditional cylindrical tube skirt worn universally by men / Paso, tied in a knot at the front, and women / Htamein, wrapped with a tuck at the side); eingyi blouse; Thanaka paste on faces.
holidays: Martyrs' Day (July 19 - commemorating General Aung San)
crafts: Traditional lacquerware (Yun) of Bagan made with horsehair and bamboo frames, gold leaf beating in Mandalay, lotus root fiber weaving at Inle Lake, and Kalaga embroidered tapestries.
worldHeritageSites: Bagan (ancient archaeological zone with over 2,000 standing Buddhist temples)
Pyu Ancient Cities (Halin, Beikthano, Sri Ksetra)

flagDescription: A horizontal tricolor consisting of three equal bands of yellow (symbolizing solidarity), green (peace, tranquility, and lush greenery), and red (courage and determination), charged in the center with a large white five-pointed star (symbolizing the union of the country).
coatOfArmsDescription: The national seal features two mythical lions (Chinthe) facing away from each other supporting a circular cartouche containing a map of Myanmar flanked by traditional floral sprigs, surmounted by a five-pointed star and enclosed by a banner inscribed "Republic of the Union of Myanmar".

landmarks: Bagan Archaeological Zone and Temple Plain
Inle Lake (leg-rowing Intha fishermen and floating gardens)
Kyaiktiyo Pagoda (Golden Rock balanced precariously on a cliff edge)
Kakku Pagoda Complex (over 2,400 stupas in Shan State)
travelNotes: Travel alerts recommend extreme caution due to active civil conflict, arbitrary detentions, and curfews; commercial flights continue into Yangon; travel outside major urban enclaves is heavily restricted; cash US dollars must be crisp and uncreased; robust offline digital tools and safety registrations advised.
shortSummary: Myanmar is an ancient and resilient Southeast Asian land of golden pagodas, sacred monasteries, and dramatic natural beauty—from the thousands of terracotta temples across the plains of Bagan to the shimmering Shwedagon Pagoda and Inle Lake—navigating a profound historic struggle for democracy.
geography: Spanning 676,578 km² across Southeast Asia. Highest point: Hkakabo Razi (5,881 m in northern Kachin State - highest peak in Southeast Asia); lowest point: Indian Ocean (0 m). Longest river: Irrawaddy River (Ayeyarwady, 2,288 km total; the lifeblood of Myanmar flowing north to south into the vast Irrawaddy Delta). Climate: Tropical monsoon; southwest monsoon season from June to September (bringing torrential rains to coastal and delta areas), cool dry season from October to February, and hot dry season from March to May with temperatures exceeding 40°C in the central dry zone.
economy: Economy with GDP nominal of $65 billion (approx. 2026) ($1,180 per capita). Leading sectors: Agriculture & Fisheries 35%, Industry & Mining 33%, Services 32%. Main industries: Natural gas extraction (offshore Yadana and Shwe fields supplying Thailand and China), Jade and gemstone mining (Hpakant jade mines - world's finest imperial jade, and Mogok rubies), Rare earth mining (Kachin State - supplying major shares of global dysprosium and terbium to China), Garment and footwear manufacturing, Timber processing and teak harvesting, Food and rice milling. Key exports: Offshore natural gas (to Thailand and China via cross-border pipelines), Garments and textiles, Pulses, beans, and sesame, Jade and gemstones, Heavy rare earth concentrates (to China), Raw rubber and rice.
culture: Rich cultural traditions featuring cuisine (Mohinga (national dish: savory rice vermicelli in a rich, fragrant broth of minced catfish, lemongrass, ginger, garlic, toasted chickpea flour, and banana tree stems, topped with crispy fritters, boiled egg, and coriander), Laphet Thoke (world-famous fermented tea leaf salad tossed with roasted peanuts, crunchy fried yellow split peas, toasted sesame seeds, garlic chips, diced tomatoes, dried shrimp, and green chilies), Shan Noodles (sticky rice noodles in spiced tomato-chicken or pork sauce), Ohn No Khao Swè (curried chicken noodle soup in coconut milk), and Burmese curries accompanied by Ngapi Yay (fermented fish dipping sauce with fresh herbs and raw vegetables).), traditional music and dance (Hsaing Waing (traditional Burmese gong and drum circle orchestra featuring the Pat Waing drum circle, Kyi Waing bronze gongs, Hne double-reed oboe, and Si bells); Saung Gauk (arched 16-stringed Burmese harp, national musical symbol of exquisite elegance); contemporary Burmese underground hip-hop and indie rock expressing anti-junta resistance.; Yein (graceful synchronized ensemble dance performed by troupes of women during Thingyan); traditional Marionette theatre (Yoke thé - puppetry that historically influenced classical dance movements).), literature (Classical Buddhist treatises and court poetry (Yadu); modern literature of Thakin Kodaw Hmaing; acclaimed contemporary writers like Pascal Khoo Thwe ("From the Land of Green Ghosts") and Ludu Daw Amar.), and sports (Chinlone (traditional non-competitive team sport where six players pass a woven rattan ball gracefully with feet, knees, and shoulders); Lethwei (traditional Burmese bare-knuckle kickboxing, renowned as the "Art of Nine Limbs" allowing headbutts, punches, kicks, elbows, and knees); Football (passionate fan base; Aung Thu).).

name: Nepal

coastline: 0 km (landlocked - nestled entirely within the Himalayas between India and China)

climate: Dramatic climatic variation within short distances: subtropical humid plains in the southern Terai, temperate in the middle hills and Kathmandu Valley, and severe polar-alpine with permanent ice in the high Himalayas
naturalHazards: Severe destructive earthquakes along the colliding Indian-Eurasian tectonic plate boundary (e.g., 2015 Gorkha earthquake)
Glacial lake outburst floods (GLOFs)
Monsoon landslides and flash flooding
environmentalIssues: Accelerated glacial melting and glacial lake outburst hazards due to global climate warming
Air quality pollution in the bowl-shaped Kathmandu Valley
Deforestation and slope erosion in the Churia hills
biodiversity: Astonishing biodiversity spanning tropical jungles to alpine peaks: home to the Royal Bengal tiger, greater one-horned rhinoceros (Chitwan National Park), snow leopard, red panda, Asian elephant, Himalayan tahr, and over 880 bird species
timeZone: UTC+05:45 (NPT - unique 45-minute offset based on the meridian of Gauri Sankar mountain)
languages: Nepali (official - Indo-Aryan language written in Devanagari script)
currency: Nepalese Rupee (NPR, रू - pegged at 1.60 NPR to 1 Indian Rupee)
legislature: Federal Parliament of Nepal (Sanghiya Sansad: National Assembly and House of Representatives / Pratinidhi Sabha)
constitution: Promulgated on September 20, 2015; established federal secular republic with seven provinces
mainPoliticalParties: Communist Party of Nepal (Unified Marxist–Leninist - CPN-UML)
Communist Party of Nepal (Maoist Centre - CPN-MC)
latestElections: Federal parliamentary elections in November 2022; coalition government reshuffle in July 2024 with K.P. Sharma Oli assuming the premiership; next general elections scheduled for 2027
politicalSituation: In July 2024, CPN-UML leader K.P. Sharma Oli formed a major coalition government with the center-left Nepali Congress party, providing parliamentary stability. The administration prioritizes constitutional governance, completing the transitional justice truth and reconciliation commissions from the 1996–2006 civil conflict, expanding cross-border hydroelectric sales to India and Bangladesh, upgrading tourist and transport infrastructure, and preparing for graduation from UN Least Developed Country (LDC) status in 2026.
foreignRelations: Maintains strict non-alignment and balanced diplomacy ("a yam between two boulders") between immediate giant neighbors India and China; major troop contributor to United Nations Peacekeeping operations worldwide; member of SAARC and BIMSTEC.
military: Nepali Army (dedicated ground defense force; international peacekeeping pillar; historic lineage of the legendary Gurkha warriors).
adminDivisions: 7 provinces: Koshi, Madhesh, Bagmati, Gandaki, Lumbini, Karnali, and Sudurpashchim, subdivided into 77 districts
history: Settled since antiquity, the Kathmandu Valley flourished under the Kirat, Licchavi (4th–8th century AD, classical golden age of architecture), and Malla dynasties (12th–18th century). The Mallas divided the valley into three rival artistic city-kingdoms: Kathmandu (Kantipur), Patan (Lalitpur), and Bhaktapur, building the UNESCO Durbar Squares. Lumbini in southern Nepal is celebrated worldwide as the sacred birthplace of Siddhartha Gautama (Gautama Buddha, born c. 563 BC). In 1768, King Prithvi Narayan Shah of Gorkha unified the disparate hill states and kingdoms, establishing the modern Kingdom of Nepal. Following the Anglo-Nepalese War (1814–1816) and the Treaty of Sugauli, the British Empire recognized Nepalese sovereignty while recruiting fearless Nepali soldiers as the famed British Gurkhas. The 1846 Kot Massacre brought the autocratic Rana Dynasty to power, ruling as hereditary prime ministers for 104 years until King Tribhuvan restored royal authority in 1951. King Mahendra introduced the non-party Panchayat system in 1960. Mass pro-democracy protests (Jana Andolan I) in 1990 restored multiparty constitutional monarchy under King Birendra. In June 2001, the tragic Royal Massacre wiped out King Birendra and his immediate family. Meanwhile, a decade-long Maoist insurgency (1996–2006) claimed over 17,000 lives, culminating in the 2006 Comprehensive Peace Accord, the abolition of the 240-year-old monarchy in 2008, and the birth of the Federal Democratic Republic of Nepal.
recentEvents2020_2026: Nepal inaugurated the Pokhara International Airport and Gautam Buddha International Airport in Bhairahawa in 2022–2023. In July 2024, K.P. Sharma Oli returned as Prime Minister leading a stable CPN-UML and Nepali Congress grand coalition. In late 2024, Nepal signed a historic trilateral power agreement with India and Bangladesh to export 40 MW of hydroelectricity across Indian transmission lines to Bangladesh. Nepal also finalized transitional justice legislation for victims of the civil conflict and made final preparations for graduation from UN Least Developed Country (LDC) status in 2026.
historicalFigures: Gautama Buddha (Siddhartha Gautama, born in Lumbini)
Tenzing Norgay Sherpa (first to summit Everest with Edmund Hillary in 1953)
Araniko (master Newar architect who built the White Pagoda in Beijing)
Bhanubhakta Acharya (Adi Kabi - Father of Nepali Literature)
ethnicGroups: Rai, Gurung, Damai, Limbu, Sherpa, and over 120 other caste and ethnic groups ~33.5%
religions: Hinduism ~81.2% (profoundly influential; Nepal was historically the world's only official Hindu kingdom until 2006)
urbanization: 22.5% (rapidly suburbanizing around Kathmandu and the Terai)
education: Tribhuvan University (oldest and largest public university in Nepal, founded 1959), Kathmandu University (KU in Dhulikhel - premier private institution), and Pokhara University; renowned international medical and engineering colleges.
healthcare: Bir Hospital, Tribhuvan University Teaching Hospital (TUTH), and Patan Hospital; expanding National Health Insurance Board (NHIB) subsidizing rural health clinics and hospital coverage.
socialCustoms: Namaste greeting with pressed palms and a slight bow; deep family hospitality; celebrating Dashain (15-day triumph of good over evil) with elders applying red Tika and Jamara to foreheads; flying kites and playing on bamboo swings (Ping); respecting sacred cows.
etiquette: Never step over someone's outstretched legs; removing shoes when entering private homes and temples; using the right hand for eating and giving gifts; touching feet of parents and elders for blessings (Dhok).
nationalIdentity: Defined by Mount Everest (Sagarmatha) and the Himalayas, the birthplace of Gautama Buddha at Lumbini, the non-rectangular national flag, martial honor of the Gurkhas, syncretic harmony between Hinduism and Buddhism, and sovereign independence never colonized by a foreign power.
sectors: Services 62% (tourism, banking, remittances, and telecommunications), Agriculture 24%, Industry & Hydropower 14%
industries: Hydroelectric power generation (rapidly expanding Himalayan run-of-the-river projects: Upper Tamakoshi, Arun III)
Mountaineering, trekking, and eco-tourism
Cement and construction materials manufacturing
Textiles, carpets, and pashmina shawls
Agro-processing (tea, cardamom, ginger, noodles)
Information technology and remote software services
agriculture: Maize, wheat, and millet in hill terraces
Large cardamom (world's #1 producer of black cardamom / Alaichi)
Buffalo milk and dairy (Chhurpi hard cheese)
naturalResources: Immense hydroelectric potential (>40,000 MW commercially viable run-of-the-river capacity)
Timber and medicinal Himalayan herbs (Yarsagumba - caterpillar fungus)
energy: Virtually 100% domestic electricity produced by renewable run-of-the-river hydropower; massive exporter of clean electricity to India during monsoon months; expanding cross-border transmission lines to Bangladesh
exports: Refined palm oil and soybean oil
imports: Petroleum fuels and LPG (from India via Motihari-Amlekhgunj pipeline)
tradePartners: India (>65% of total goods trade, free bilateral transit)
China (expanding northern mountain border crossings: Tatopani, Rasuwagadhi)
United States (top market for carpets and handicrafts)
tourism: Surpassed 1.3 million international tourists drawn to mountaineering expeditions on Mount Everest and the Annapurna Circuit, trekking in Langtang and Manaslu, serene lakes and paragliding in Pokhara, wildlife jungle safaris in Chitwan (rhinos and tigers), and ancient Durbar Squares of Kathmandu.
employment: Remittances sent by over 3 million Nepali migrant workers in the Gulf states, Malaysia, and worldwide exceed $10 billion annually (~25% of GDP); growing employment in tourism, civil engineering, and IT.
debtInflation: Nepal Rastra Bank maintains the currency peg to the Indian Rupee (1.60 NPR = 1 INR); robust foreign exchange reserves exceeding $14 billion; inflation tracking Indian price levels around 5-6%.
transport: Tribhuvan Highway and Prithvi Highway connecting Kathmandu to the Terai and Pokhara; Mugling-Pokhara highway four-lane expansion; Narayangarh-Butwal highway; domestic STOL mountain flights (Lukla Tenzing-Hillary Airport, gateway to Everest).
ports: Landlocked; relies on Indian seaports of Kolkata/Haldia and Visakhapatnam for international container maritime cargo via the Birgunj Integrated Check Post (ICP) rail dry port
internetUsage: 52.5% (expanding fiber-to-the-home networks and 4G/5G mobile connectivity, widespread digital payments via eSewa, Khalti, and Fonepay QR)
cuisine: Dal Bhat Tarkari (the beloved national dish eaten twice daily: steamed white rice served with seasoned yellow lentil soup / Dal, spiced seasonal vegetable curry / Tarkari, tomato cilantro achar, and spicy greens / Saag), Momo (legendary steamed or fried dumplings filled with spiced buffalo, chicken, or vegetables, served with fiery sesame-tomato chutney / Golbheda ko Achar), Gundruk (fermented leafy green vegetable soup, iconic Nepali comfort food), Sel Roti (sweet, crispy ring-shaped fried rice-flour bread made during festivals), Thukpa (hearty Tibetan-style noodle soup), Yomari (steamed Newar rice-flour pastry filled with sweet Chaku molasses and sesame), and spicy Choila (charcoal-grilled marinated buffalo meat).
festivals: Dashain / Bijaya Dashami (grandest 15-day national festival celebrating the victory of goddess Durga)
Tihar / Deepawali (Festival of Lights: five days honoring crows, dogs, cows, oxen, and sisters through Bhai Tika)
Maha Shivaratri (massive gathering of hundreds of thousands of sadhus and pilgrims at Pashupatinath Temple)
Buddha Jayanti (celebrating Buddha's birth in Lumbini)
Indra Jatra (Kathmandu festival featuring the chariot procession of the living goddess Kumari)
music: Traditional folk music (Lok Dohori - playful improvised singing duels between men and women); Sarangi (four-stringed bowed lute played by the Gandharbha caste); Madal (traditional double-ended hand drum, heartbeat of Nepali folk music); Bansuri (bamboo flute); vibrant contemporary Nepali folk-rock (Nepathya, 1974 AD).
dance: Maruni dance, Lakhey masked demon dance (performed during Indra Jatra in Kathmandu), Tamang Selo, Chandi dance (Rai community), and Sorathi dance.
art: Newar Paubha painting (intricate traditional religious scroll painting depicting Hindu and Buddhist deities); Newari woodcarving (intricately carved wooden peacocks, struts, and window lattices of Bhaktapur); lost-wax bronze metal sculpture; Thangka painting.
architecture: Distinctive multi-roofed Newar pagoda temple architecture (Nyatapola Temple in Bhaktapur, Kasthamandap); massive hemispherical Buddhist stupas with serene all-seeing eyes of the Buddha (Boudhanath and Swayambhunath); ancient Durbar Squares of Kathmandu, Patan, and Bhaktapur.
literature: Bhanubhakta Acharya (translated the Valmiki Ramayana into vernacular Nepali, unifying the literary language); Laxmi Prasad Devkota ("The Great Poet" / Mahakavi: "Muna Madan", the best-selling book in Nepali literature); Parijat ("Siris ko Phool" / The Blue Mimosa); modern authors Samrat Upadhyay and Manjushree Thapa.
cinema: Emerging Nepali cinema ("Kollywood"); acclaimed international festival-winning independent directors: Min Bahadur Bham ("The Black Hen", "Shambhala" - historic premiere at the 2024 Berlin International Film Festival) and Nabin Subba ("A Road to a Village").
sports: Cricket is an immense national passion (the Nepali national cricket team "Rhinos" qualified for the ICC Men's T20 World Cup in 2024 amidst wild domestic euphoria); Football (packed Dasharath Stadium); Mountaineering and Trail Running (world-record mountain athlete Mira Rai; Nirmal "Nimsdai" Purja who summited all 14 eight-thousanders in 6 months); Volleyball (national sport).
media: Kantipur Publications, The Kathmandu Post, Republica, Onlinekhabar, Setopati, Nepal Television (NTV), and Kantipur TV.
clothing: Daura-Suruwal (traditional tunic and trousers with tailored Dhaka topi geometric woven hat and coat for men); Gunyou-Cholo or vibrant red and green Sarees for women; Bakkhu wool coats and Pangden aprons worn by Sherpa women in the high mountains.
crafts: Handwoven Dhaka fabric (Dhaka topi hats and shawls from Palpa), handmade Lokta Daphne bush paper, hand-knotted Tibetan wool carpets, silver filigree jewelry, and singing bowls.
worldHeritageSites: Kathmandu Valley (seven monument zones: Durbar Squares of Kathmandu, Patan, Bhaktapur; Swayambhunath, Boudhanath, Pashupatinath, Changu Narayan)
Lumbini, the Birthplace of the Lord Buddha

flagDescription: The world's only non-quadrilateral national flag: a combination of two vertical red triangular pennants bordered in deep blue; the upper pennant bears a white stylized crescent moon with eight rays, and the lower pennant bears a white twelve-pointed sun (symbolizing the desire for the nation to endure as long as the sun and moon).

name: North Korea
nationalDay: September 9 (Day of the Foundation of the Republic in 1948)
motto: Powerful and Prosperous Nation (강성대국 - Gangseong Daeguk)
borders: South Korea (divided by the 4 km wide Demilitarized Zone / DMZ along the 38th parallel)
coastline: 2,495 km (Sea of Japan / East Sea of Korea to the east, and Yellow Sea / West Sea of Korea to the west)
highestPoint: Paektu Mountain (Mount Paektu, 2,744 m - sacred active stratovolcano on the Chinese border, cradling Heaven Lake)
lowestPoint: Sea of Japan / Yellow Sea (0 m)

majorMountains: Mount Kumgang (Diamond Mountain, 1,638 m - famed for dramatic granite pinnacles)
climate: Humid continental; short, hot, humid summers and long, bitterly cold, snowy winters influenced by Siberian air masses
naturalHazards: Severe droughts followed by seasonal monsoon flash flooding causing agricultural crop damage
Spring dust storms from the Gobi
environmentalIssues: Deforestation on hillside slopes from past wood-fuel harvesting
Soil erosion and land degradation impacting cereal crop yields
Air pollution from heavy coal-fired industrial heating
biodiversity: Rugged mountain forests harbor the Siberian (Amur) tiger, Amur leopard, Asiatic black bear, Manchurian sika deer, red-crowned crane, and pristine subalpine flora around Mount Paektu
languages: Korean (Munhwa'ŏ / Cultural Language - official state standard)
government: Unitary one-party socialist state / totalitarian hereditary dictatorship
headOfState: President of State Affairs Kim Jong Un (General Secretary of the Workers' Party of Korea); Chairman of the Standing Committee of the Supreme People's Assembly Choe Ryong Hae (represents state diplomatically)
legislature: Supreme People's Assembly (SPA - unicameral 687-seat parliament)
constitution: Adopted in 1972; amended repeatedly (incorporating Juche, Songun, and nuclear state status, with Kimilsungism-Kimjongilism as state ideology)
mainPoliticalParties: Workers' Party of Korea (WPK - sole ruling party)
Democratic Front for the Reunification of Korea (including minor satellite groups: Korean Social Democratic Party, Chondoist Chongu Party)
latestElections: 14th Supreme People's Assembly election in March 2019; 8th Congress of the Workers' Party of Korea in 2021
politicalSituation: Under Supreme Leader Kim Jong Un, North Korea has consolidated its status as a de facto nuclear-weapon state, enshrining nuclear status irrevocably in its constitution and advancing intercontinental ballistic missiles (Hwasong-17/18), hypersonic gliders, and military reconnaissance satellites. In 2024, North Korea formally abandoned the long-standing goal of peaceful reunification with South Korea, declaring the South its "principal enemy", and signed a historic Comprehensive Strategic Partnership Treaty with Russia in June 2024 (including a mutual defense assistance pact), expanding geopolitical and military cooperation.
foreignRelations: Deep strategic, military, and economic alliance with the Russian Federation (formal mutual defense pact signed in 2024); comprehensive friendship and economic trade lifeline with China; adversarial relations with the United States, South Korea, and Japan; subject to comprehensive UN Security Council sanctions.
military: Korean People's Army (KPA: Ground Force, Navy, Air and Anti-Air Force, Strategic Rocket Force, and Special Operation Force; world's 4th largest active standing military with ~1.2 million personnel; nuclear weapons capability and extensive artillery batteries).
internationalOrgs: UN (admitted simultaneously with South Korea in 1991)
adminDivisions: 9 provinces (do), 1 direct-administered city (Pyongyang), 3 special cities (Nampo, Rason, Kaesong)
history: Korean civilization traces to the mythical founding of Gojoseon by Dangun in 2333 BC. The Three Kingdoms of Korea (Goguryeo, Baekje, and Silla) competed for supremacy; northern Goguryeo was renowned for military power and vast Manchurian territories. Following unified Silla and the Goryeo Dynasty (which gave Korea its Western name and invented metal movable type in 1234), the Joseon Dynasty (1392–1910) established Confucian statecraft and King Sejong the Great created the Hangul alphabet in 1443. Following the Japanese annexation of Korea in 1910 and brutal colonial rule, Kim Il Sung led anti-Japanese guerrilla resistance in Manchuria. At the conclusion of World War II in 1945, the Korean Peninsula was divided along the 38th parallel into Soviet and American occupation zones. The Democratic People's Republic of Korea was proclaimed on September 9, 1948, under Kim Il Sung. On June 25, 1950, North Korea launched a full-scale invasion of the South, starting the devastating Korean War (1950–1953). UN forces led by the US intervened on behalf of the South, while the Chinese People's Volunteer Army intervened for the North. The war ended on July 27, 1953, with an armistice (not a permanent peace treaty), establishing the heavily fortified Demilitarized Zone (DMZ). Kim Il Sung established the autarkic ideology of Juche (self-reliance), centralizing power through the Chollima economic movement. Following the collapse of the Soviet Union, North Korea endured a catastrophic famine in the 1990s ("The Arduous March"). Kim Jong Il instituted the "Songun" (military-first) doctrine and conducted North Korea's first nuclear test in 2006. Kim Jong Un assumed power in December 2011, accelerating missile and nuclear miniaturization programs.
recentEvents2020_2026: North Korea maintained near-total international border closures during 2020–2023, subsequently reopening trade with China and Russia. In September 2023, Kim Jong Un traveled to Russia for a summit with Vladimir Putin, followed by Russian President Putin visiting Pyongyang in June 2024 to sign the landmark Comprehensive Strategic Partnership Treaty pledging mutual military assistance in case of aggression. Domestically, North Korea dismantled the Monument to the Three Charters for National Reunification in Pyongyang after officially declaring South Korea an irreconcilable hostile state, conducted successful launches of the Malligyong-1 military spy satellite, and accelerated construction of 50,000 modern residential flats in Pyongyang.
historicalFigures: Kim Jong Un (President of State Affairs)
ethnicGroups: Korean ~99.8% (one of the world's most ethnically homogeneous societies)
Small Chinese community and tiny resident Japanese diaspora ~0.2%
religions: Officially atheist state; traditional Korean shamanism, Buddhism, and Chondoism (Religion of the Heavenly Way) preserved under state oversight; organized religious activities strictly regulated
education: Kim Il Sung University, Kim Chaek University of Technology (premier engineering institution), and Pyongyang University of Foreign Studies; universal state-funded compulsory 12-year basic and secondary education.
healthcare: Nominally free universal healthcare system under the Ministry of Public Health; village clinics and district polyclinics supported by Traditional Korean Medicine (Koryo medicine) alongside modern pharmaceuticals.
socialCustoms: Immense state loyalty and reverence for the Kim leadership dynasty; wearing leadership badges (Kim Il Sung and Kim Jong Il lapel pins) over the heart; communal work brigades; Sunday neighborhood clean-up campaigns.
etiquette: Showing paramount respect to leadership portraits and national monuments (bowing before statues at Mansu Hill); bowing slightly to elders and superiors; polite speech registers in Korean.
nationalIdentity: Formed through the Juche ideology of national self-reliance, martial pride in military might and nuclear deterrence, shared Korean cultural roots, and collective unity under the Supreme Leader.
sectors: Industry, Metallurgy & Mining 46%, Services 32%, Agriculture & Fisheries 22%
industries: Military defense equipment, ammunition, and missile assembly
Anthracite coal and mineral mining
Ferrous and non-ferrous metallurgy (steel, iron, lead, zinc)
Chemical manufacturing and synthetic fibers (Vinalon - the "Juche fiber")
Cement and heavy construction
Textile sewing and light consumer manufacturing
agriculture: Rice (irrigated paddy fields in western coastal plains)
naturalResources: Vast coal deposits (anthracite and thermal coal)
Iron ore (Musan iron mine - one of the largest in Asia)
energy: Dominated by coal-fired thermal power and hydroelectric river dams (Supung Dam, Huichon power stations); persistent domestic electricity shortages managed through rolling grid rationing and widespread small rooftop solar PV panels in residential towns
exports: Anthracite coal, iron ore, and minerals (primarily to China under regulatory quotas)
Defense materiel and munitions (to Russia under bilateral strategic treaties)
imports: Crude petroleum and refined fuels (via pipelines from China and rail from Russia)
tradePartners: China (>90% of formal recorded external trade)
Russia (rapidly expanding strategic, logistics, and energy trade post-2023)
tourism: Regulated state tourism operating through Korea International Travel Company (KITC); foreign visitors travel on strictly guided itineraries visiting Pyongyang, the DMZ at Panmunjom, Mount Myohyang, and Kaesong.
employment: Universal state employment allocation in collective farms, state-owned enterprises, armed forces, or municipal construction brigades; informal consumer market trading (Jangmadang).
debtInflation: Dual-currency reality with widespread domestic circulation of Chinese Yuan (RMB) and US Dollars in markets alongside official North Korean Won; state banks promoting electronic electronic card transactions (Narae card).
transport: State railway network (electrified mainline linking Pyongyang to Sinuiju/China, Tumangang/Russia, and coastal industrial zones); Pyongyang Metro (one of the deepest subways in the world, over 100m underground, doubling as a bomb shelter); trolleybuses and trams in Pyongyang.
airports: Pyongyang Sunan International Airport (FNJ - modern terminal hub for state airline Air Koryo)
ports: Port of Nampo (primary western maritime gateway with the massive 8 km West Sea Barrage)
Port of Rason (Rajin - ice-free northeastern port with direct rail to Russia)
Port of Chongjin
Port of Wonsan
internetUsage: <1.0% access to global internet (restricted to top state, scientific, and security leadership); widespread domestic intranet (Kwangmyong) accessible via desktop terminals and domestic smartphones (Pyongyang, Arirang models)
cuisine: Cold Noodles / Pyongyang Naengmyeon (famous national dish: chewy buckwheat noodles served in chilled, tangy beef and pheasant broth with dongchimi radish water, topped with sliced beef, boiled egg, and mustard), Pyongyang Onban (warm rice dish topped with shredded chicken, mung bean pancakes, and mushrooms in savory chicken broth), Kimchi (crisp, refreshing, less spicy northern variety made with cabbage and radishes), Kaesong Pyeonsu (square dumplings filled with vegetables and beef), Taedong River mullet soup (Taedonggang Suno-guk), and sweet Songpyeon rice cakes.
festivals: Day of the Sun (April 15 - Birthday of Kim Il Sung, grandest state holiday)
Day of the Shining Star (February 16 - Birthday of Kim Jong Il)
Day of the Foundation of the Republic (September 9)
Mass Games and artistic performances (Arirang festival legacy)
music: Massive revolutionary choral and orchestral music (State Merited Chorus, Moranbong Band - all-female electric pop group, Samjiyon Orchestra); folk songs played on the Kayagum and Okryugum (modernized zither created in North Korea); traditional Arirang folk melody.
dance: Mass synchronised dance displays performed in Kim Il Sung Square by thousands of college students in colorful traditional attire; classical Korean fan dance (Buchaechum) and sword dance.
art: Socialist Realism and Chosonhwa (traditional Korean ink wash painting technique adapted with vibrant, realistic oil-like colors depicting revolutionary themes, workers, soldiers, and Mount Paektu); monumental bronze sculpture from the Mansudae Art Studio (one of the largest art production centers in the world).
architecture: Monumental neoclassical and socialist architecture in Pyongyang: Juche Tower (170-meter granite needle crowned by an illuminated red torch), Grand People's Study House, Triumph Arch (larger than the Arc de Triomphe in Paris), Ryugyong Hotel (105-story pyramid skyscraper), and the Kumsusan Palace of the Sun (mausoleum of Kim Il Sung and Kim Jong Il); historic wooden Joseon dynasty gates in Kaesong.
literature: Revolutionary literary fiction and dramatic plays patronized by the state ("The Sea of Blood", "The Flower Girl"); classical Korean poetry and historical chronicles.
cinema: The North Korean film industry produced classics like "The Flower Girl" (1972) and martial arts movie "Hong Kil Dong" (1986); cinematic treatises authored by Kim Jong Il ("On the Art of the Cinema").
sports: Weightlifting (global Olympic powerhouse: multiple Olympic Gold medals and world records won by Om Yun-chol, Rim Jong-sim, and world-record performances in 2024); Women's Football (world champions at youth levels, multi-time AFC Women's Asian Cup champions); Table Tennis (historic mixed doubles Olympic silver medal at Paris 2024); Gymnastics; Taekwondo (ITF - International Taekwon-Do Federation headquarters in Pyongyang).
media: Korean Central News Agency (KCNA - official state news agency), Rodong Sinmun (Newspaper of the Central Committee of the WPK), and Korean Central Television (KCTV).
clothing: Joseon-ot (traditional Korean dress: Chima skirt and Jeogori jacket in vibrant colors worn for state holidays and formal events); functional modern suits, dark coats, and Mao-style tunics (Inminbok) worn by men; military uniforms ubiquitous across all levels of society.
crafts: Traditional Korean mother-of-pearl lacquerware, Koryo celadon ceramics, handwoven silk, and Kaesong Insam (Ginseng) tonics and extracts.

Historic Monuments and Sites in Kaesong (Manwoldae palace, Kaesong Chomsongdae observatory, Sungkyunkwan academy)

coatOfArmsDescription: A national emblem depicting a massive hydroelectric power plant beneath the glowing five-pointed red star of socialism, framed by ears of ripe rice tied with a red ribbon bearing the inscription "Democratic People's Republic of Korea" in Chosŏn'gŭl script.

name: Oman
nationalDay: November 18 (National Day - Birthday of late Sultan Qaboos)
motto: None (Unofficial: Peace, Heritage, and Harmony)
coastline: 3,165 km (Arabian Sea, Gulf of Oman, and the strategic Strait of Hormuz at Musandam)
highestPoint: Jabal Shams (Mountain of the Sun, 3,009 m in the Hajar Mountains)
longestRiver: None (no permanent rivers; seasonal flowing wadis: Wadi Shab, Wadi Bani Khalid, Wadi Tiwi)

climate: Arid desert and subtropical; hot and dry interior; hot and humid coastal plains; Dhofar region in the south experiences the unique summer monsoon (Khareef) from June to September, turning the arid mountains into lush, mist-shrouded green paradises

Flash flooding in narrow rocky mountain wadis
Periodic summer sandstorms

Preservation of fragile coastal mangrove lagoons and coral reefs
Overgrazing and desertification in southern rangelands
biodiversity: Remarkable Arabian biodiversity: Arabian oryx sanctuary (reintroduced into the wild), Arabian leopard (critically endangered in Dhofar's Jabal Samhan), green sea turtle nesting sanctuaries at Ras al Jinz, Arabian humpback whales, and frankincense trees (Boswellia sacra)
languages: English (widely spoken in commerce, business, and tourism)
Balochi, Lawati, and South Arabian indigenous languages (Mehri, Shehri/Jibbali in Dhofar)
currency: Omani Rial (OMR, ر.ع. - 3rd highest-valued currency in the world: pegged at 1 OMR = 2.60 USD)
headOfGovernment: Prime Minister Haitham bin Tariq (held by the Sultan)
legislature: Council of Oman (Majlis Oman: appointed State Council / Majlis al-Dawla, and elected Consultative Council / Majlis al-Shura)
constitution: Basic Statute of the State (promulgated in 1996; revised in 2021 to establish a designated Crown Prince)
mainPoliticalParties: Political parties are constitutionally prohibited; citizens elect the 90 members of the Consultative Council via direct universal suffrage
latestElections: Consultative Council (Majlis al-Shura) elections in October 2023 (conducted 100% digitally via the "Intakhib" smartphone app); municipal council elections in 2022
politicalSituation: Under Sultan Haitham bin Tariq (who succeeded the beloved late Sultan Qaboos bin Said in January 2020), Oman is methodically executing its "Oman Vision 2040" transformation. The administration achieved substantial fiscal stabilization, eliminated sovereign budget deficits, reduced public debt, and designated Crown Prince Theyazin bin Haitham. Internationally, Oman remains the universally trusted diplomatic mediator ("Switzerland of the Middle East"), brokering delicate negotiations between Western nations, Iran, Saudi Arabia, and regional factions.
foreignRelations: Founding member of the GCC, Arab League, and UN; renowned for constructive neutrality, independent foreign policy, and backchannel diplomatic mediation (facilitating the 2015 JCPOA Iran nuclear talks and regional hostage releases); strategic defense agreements with the United Kingdom and United States.
military: Sultan of Oman's Armed Forces (Royal Army of Oman, Royal Air Force of Oman with Eurofighter Typhoon and F-16 jets, Royal Navy of Oman commanding the Strait of Hormuz, and Royal Guard of Oman).
adminDivisions: 11 governorates (muhafazat): Muscat, Dhofar, Musandam, Buraimi, Dakhiliyah, Batinah North, Batinah South, Sharqiyah North, Sharqiyah South, Dhahirah, and Wusta
history: Oman was an ancient center of copper mining and maritime trade known to the Sumerians as "Magan" in the 3rd millennium BC. It was also the cradle of the ancient Frankincense Trade, where fragrant resin harvested from Boswellia trees in Dhofar was transported across caravan and sea routes to Rome, Egypt, and India. Oman was one of the earliest lands to embrace Islam peacefully in 630 AD during the lifetime of Prophet Muhammad. The Ibadi school of Islam established an elective Imamate in the interior mountains in the 8th century, which coexisted with maritime sultanates on the coast. In 1507, Portuguese explorer Afonso de Albuquerque conquered Muscat and coastal ports, fortifying them with forts Al Jalali and Al Mirani. The Yaruba Dynasty expelled the Portuguese in 1650, building a formidable maritime empire. In 1744, Ahmad bin Said al-Busaidi founded the current Al Said Dynasty. In the 19th century, under Sultan Said bin Sultan, the Omani Empire reached its zenith, controlling Zanzibar, parts of the East African coast, and Gwadar (in modern Pakistan), making Zanzibar the co-capital of the empire. Following his death, the realm was divided into the Sultanate of Zanzibar and the Sultanate of Muscat and Oman. Sultan Qaboos bin Said overthrew his father in 1970, launching the "Omani Renaissance", uniting the country, ending the Dhofar rebellion, and transforming an impoverished state with only 10 km of paved roads into a modern, prosperous nation while preserving traditional Arabian architecture and cultural heritage.
recentEvents2020_2026: Sultan Qaboos passed away peacefully in January 2020 after 50 years of visionary rule, succeeded smoothly by his cousin Sultan Haitham bin Tariq. Sultan Haitham reformed governance under Royal Decree 6/2021, creating the formal role of Crown Prince (conferred on his son Sayyid Theyazin bin Haitham). Between 2022 and 2026, Oman turned sovereign debt into investment-grade fiscal surpluses, developed the multi-billion-dollar Special Economic Zone at Duqm (including the modern Duqm Refinery), signed landmark green hydrogen and ammonia export agreements through "Hydrom" attracting >$30 billion in international commitments, and served as chief mediator in ceasefire and humanitarian talks for Yemen.
historicalFigures: Sultan Qaboos bin Said (Architect of Modern Oman)
Ahmad bin Said al-Busaidi (Founder of Al Said Dynasty)
Said bin Sultan (Ruler of Omani-Zanzibar Empire)
Ahmad ibn Majid (legendary 15th-century Omani navigator and cartographer)
ethnicGroups: Omani citizens ~58% (Arab heritage, with historical Swahili, Balochi, and Lawati communities reflecting maritime empire roots)
Expatriate residents ~42% (predominantly Indian, Bangladeshi, Pakistani, Egyptian, and Filipino professionals)
religions: Islam ~85.9% (predominantly Ibadi Islam ~45%, Sunni ~45%, Shia ~5%; renowned for exemplary sectarian tolerance and peaceful coexistence)
education: Sultan Qaboos University (SQU in Al Khoudh - premier national research university), University of Nizwa, and German University of Technology in Oman (GUtech); primary and secondary education free for all Omani citizens.
healthcare: Comprehensive universal healthcare provided by the Ministry of Health through modern regional hospitals (Royal Hospital and Khoula Hospital in Muscat, Sultan Qaboos Hospital in Salalah); recognized by the WHO for world-leading efficiency in health service delivery.
socialCustoms: Coffee and dates hospitality: serving Omani Kahwa (coffee flavored with cardamom and saffron) accompanied by fresh dates and Halwa; wearing national dress with pride; gathering at the Sablah (communal village council hall) for weddings, funerals, and social discussions.
etiquette: Warm handshakes; accepting coffee and dates with the right hand; shaking the small cup gently from side to side when finished; conservative modesty in public spaces; high respect for elders and royal decrees.
nationalIdentity: Deeply anchored in maritime seafaring heritage, ancient frankincense trade legacy, peaceful and tolerant Ibadi Islamic values, unique architectural aesthetics avoiding garish skyscrapers, and national pride in modernization without losing cultural soul.
sectors: Oil & Hydrocarbons 33%, Services & Logistics 50%, Manufacturing & Mining 15%, Agriculture & Fisheries 2%
industries: Crude petroleum and natural gas extraction (Petroleum Development Oman - PDO)
Liquefied natural gas (Oman LNG in Sur)
Petroleum refining and petrochemicals (OQ: Duqm Refinery, Sohar Refinery)
Green hydrogen and ammonia development (Hydrom)
Port logistics and maritime transshipment (Salalah, Sohar, Duqm)
Aluminum smelting (Sohar Aluminium)
Mining (limestone, gypsum, copper)
agriculture: Dates (over 8 million date palms producing premium Fardh and Khalas varieties)
Pomegranates, walnuts, and roses (Jabal Akhdar mountain terraces)
naturalResources: Natural gas deposits (Khazzan tight gas mega-field)
World-class solar and wind energy resources (among the highest photovoltaic irradiance globally)
energy: Dominated by natural gas; executing an aggressive green hydrogen roadmap targeting 1 million tonnes of green hydrogen annually by 2030 through massive wind and solar concessions in Duqm and Dhofar; operational Ibri II 500 MW solar park and Amin solar park
imports: Transport motor vehicles and spare parts
tradePartners: China (largest crude oil buyer, purchasing >80% of Omani oil exports)
India (major bilateral trade and investment partner)
tourism: Surpassed 4.2 million international tourists drawn to Muscat's white architecture and Royal Opera House, historic mud-brick forts of Nizwa and Bahla, wadi canyoning in Wadi Shab and Bimmah Sinkhole, turtle watching at Ras al Jinz, dramatic fjords of Musandam ("Norway of Arabia"), and the lush green summer Khareef season in Salalah.
employment: Omanization policy systematically increasing citizen participation in the private workforce; expanding private banking, fintech, renewable engineering, and tourism sectors; low unemployment among citizens (~3.8%).
debtInflation: Strong sovereign balance sheet; public debt declined to ~35% of GDP; sovereign wealth assets managed by Oman Investment Authority (OIA) exceeding $50 billion; inflation maintained low at ~1.5%.
transport: Oman-Etihad Rail (Hafeet Rail connecting Sohar Port to Abu Dhabi via high-speed freight and passenger rail); modern 8-lane expressways (Muscat Expressway, Batinah Expressway); state-of-the-art Muscat International Airport; passenger and vehicle catamarans operated by National Ferries Company.
airports: Muscat International Airport (MCT - award-winning modern terminal designed for 20M passengers, hub of Oman Air)
ports: Port of Salalah (world-class transshipment container hub on the Indian Ocean)
Port of Sohar (deepwater industrial and bulk container port)
Port of Duqm (mega multi-purpose port, drydock, and naval facility)
Port Sultan Qaboos (cruise and maritime tourism hub in Muscat)
cuisine: Shuwa (legendary national culinary masterpiece: bone-in lamb or goat marinated in a rich, fiery paste of dates, coriander, cumin, red chili, and vinegar, wrapped in banana or palm leaves, placed inside a woven palm-frond sack, and slow-roasted for 24 to 48 hours in a communal underground sand pit oven, served at Eid over fragrant spiced saffron rice), Majboos / Kabsa (fragrant rice cooked with meat and dried black lime), Mashuai (spit-roasted kingfish served with lemon rice), Harees (slow-cooked wheat and meat porridge), and Omani Halwa (world-famous sweet delicacy made from starch, caramelized sugar, clarified butter / Ghee, saffron, cardamom, and rosewater, topped with toasted almonds and cashews, served hot with bitter black cardamom coffee).
festivals: Salalah Tourism Festival (celebrating the misty green Khareef season from July to August with music and cultural events)
Muscat Festival (annual cultural arts and heritage festival)
Eid al-Fitr and Eid al-Adha (marked by communal Shuwa feasts)
music: Traditional Omani music incorporating Arabian, East African, and Persian musical influences; Razha (traditional musical poetry duel accompanied by sword tossing); Oud playing; world-class classical symphony orchestra (Royal Oman Symphony Orchestra - ROSO, founded by Sultan Qaboos).
dance: Razha and Ayyala sword dances (performed by men in rows reciting poetry and Brandishing swords); Liwa and Dan (vibrant drumming dances reflecting East African seafaring heritage); Dhofari female folk dances.
art: Bait Al Zubair and National Museum of Oman; exquisite Islamic calligraphy, silver dagger craftsmanship, contemporary Omani fine art at the Omani Society for Fine Arts.
architecture: Strict municipal building codes preserving authentic Omani white and cream Islamic architecture with arched windows, crenellated rooflines, and carved wooden doors (skyscrapers are prohibited in Muscat); Sultan Qaboos Grand Mosque (monumental white marble mosque featuring a 50m golden dome, 8.5-ton Swarovski crystal chandelier, and a handwoven Persian carpet); Royal Opera House Muscat (stunning marble and teakwood cultural palace); UNESCO mud-brick fortress of Bahla Fort and Nizwa Fort with its massive round tower.
literature: Centuries of Islamic scholarship and navigational literature (Ahmad ibn Majid's nautical treatises); modern Omani literature: Jokha Alharthi (author of "Celestial Bodies", first Arabic-language novel to win the prestigious International Booker Prize in 2019); poetry of Saif Ghobash.
cinema: Emerging cinema scene supported by the Muscat International Film Festival and Oman Film and Theatre Society; international filming location for desert and maritime features.
sports: Football (Oman won the Arabian Gulf Cup in 2009 and 2017; legendary goalkeeper Ali Al-Habsi played in the English Premier League); Camel Racing (prestigious traditional races with robotic jockeys); Traditional Dhow Sailing and modern oceanic sailing (Oman Sail); Horse Riding and Showjumping.
media: Oman News Agency (ONA), Oman Daily Observer (English daily), Times of Oman, Oman Daily (Arabic), and Oman TV.
clothing: Men wear the Dishdasha (collarless white or muted pastel robe featuring a delicate short tassel called Farakha / Tarboosha lightly scented with perfume) paired with the embroidered Kumma round cap or Mussar wool turban, and for formal events the ceremonial silver Khanjar (curved dagger) tucked into an embroidered belt; women wear vibrant embroidered tunics with matching trousers (Sirwal) and Shayla headscarf, or elegant black Abayas.
crafts: Omani Khanjar silversmithing (UNESCO Intangible Cultural Heritage), Bahla traditional pottery (UNESCO), copper coffeepot making (Dallah), rosewater distillation on Jabal Akhdar, and palm-leaf weaving.
worldHeritageSites: Archaeological Sites of Bat, Al-Khutm and Al-Ayn
Land of Frankincense (Wadi Dawkah, Shisr/Ubar, Sumhuram, Al-Baleed)
Aflaj Irrigation Systems of Oman (ancient 2,000-year-old gravity water channels)

Date palm, knowledge, skills, traditions and practices

Land of Frankincense sites and Salalah coastal Khareef

The Special Investment Facilitation Council (SIFC) is driving foreign investment from GCC partners (Saudi Arabia, UAE, Qatar) and China into mining (Reko Diq copper-gold project), energy, and agriculture, while managing domestic political tensions and cross-border security challenges along the Afghan and Iranian borders.

history: Pakistan is home to the ancient Indus Valley Civilization (c. 3300–1300 BC), centered at Mohenjo-daro and Harappa, pioneering urban drainage, brick architecture, and standardized weights. Gandhara blossomed as a global hub of Greco-Buddhist art in Taxila (conquered by Alexander the Great in 326 BC) under the Kushan Empire. Muhammad bin Qasim introduced Islam to Sindh ("Bab-ul-Islam" / Gateway of Islam) in 711 AD. The region flourished under the Delhi Sultanate and reached an artistic, imperial peak under the Mughal Empire, with Lahore serving as imperial capital under Akbar and Jahangir (constructing the Badshahi Mosque, Lahore Fort, and Shalimar Gardens). Following the fall of the Sikh Empire in 1849, the British Raj annexed the territory. The Pakistan Movement, conceptualized by philosopher-poet Allama Muhammad Iqbal in 1930 and championed by Muhammad Ali Jinnah (Quaid-e-Azam / Great Leader) through the All-India Muslim League, secured the creation of Pakistan as an independent homeland for Muslims on August 14, 1947, through the Partition of British India. Originally consisting of West and East Pakistan, the eastern wing seceded in 1971 following a tragic civil war to become Bangladesh. Under Zulfikar Ali Bhutto, Pakistan adopted its 1973 democratic constitution and initiated its nuclear program, successfully conducting nuclear tests in 1998 (Youm-e-Takbeer). Modern political history has cycled between democratic civilian administrations and military governments (Ayub Khan, Zia-ul-Haq, Pervez Musharraf).

In February 2024, Pakistan held highly competitive general elections leading to a coalition government headed by Shehbaz Sharif. Between 2024 and 2026, Pakistan secured a critical $7 billion IMF stabilization package, advanced commercial development of the monumental Reko Diq copper-gold project in Balochistan with Barrick Gold, inaugurated the upgraded Gwadar International Airport under CPEC, and celebrated national pride in Olympic javelin champion Arshad Nadeem.

history: Palestine possesses an unbroken multi-millennial history as a crossroads of civilizations. Jericho (Tell es-Sultan) is recognized as the oldest continuously inhabited walled city on Earth, dating back over 11,000 years (Neolithic era). The Canaanites established city-states in the 3rd millennium BC, followed by the Philistines along the southern coast. The land holds supreme spiritual sanctity in Judaism, Christianity, and Islam: Jesus Christ was born in Bethlehem and preached throughout the region; for Muslims, Jerusalem (Al-Quds) is the first Qibla and third holiest city, where the Prophet Muhammad ascended to heaven during the Isra and Mi'raj from the Al-Aqsa Mosque and Dome of the Rock. Ruled successively by ancient Israelites, Assyrians, Babylonians, Persians, Romans, and Byzantines, the territory came under Islamic rule in 637 AD when Caliph Umar ibn al-Khattab entered Jerusalem, issuing the peaceful Assurance of Umar. The Crusader period (1099–1187) ended when Saladin (Salah ad-Din) recaptured Jerusalem. Centuries of Mamluk and Ottoman rule (1516–1917) integrated Palestine into regional trade, famed for olive oil, Nabulsi soap, and citrus exports. Following World War I, Britain governed under the League of Nations Mandate for Palestine. The UN General Assembly adopted Resolution 181 in 1947 proposing partition, followed by the 1948 war and the "Nakba" (Catastrophe), in which over 700,000 Palestinians were displaced from their homes, becoming refugees. In 1967 (the Six-Day War), Israel occupied the West Bank, East Jerusalem, and the Gaza Strip. The Palestine Liberation Organization (PLO) under Yasser Arafat was recognized as the sole legitimate representative of the Palestinian people in 1974. The First Intifada (1987) led to the 1993 Oslo Accords, establishing the Palestinian National Authority with interim autonomy. The failure of final status talks led to the Second Intifada (2000–2005). In 2012, the UN General Assembly voted overwhelmingly to grant Palestine Non-Member Observer State status.
recentEvents2020_2026: The October 7, 2023 attacks and the resulting catastrophic war in the Gaza Strip caused unprecedented civilian devastation, displacing over 1.9 million Palestinians, leveling over 60% of Gaza's housing infrastructure, and killing over 43,000 people according to local health authorities. In 2024, the International Court of Justice (ICJ) issued landmark advisory opinions regarding the illegality of the occupation, and the International Criminal Court (ICC) sought arrest warrants. In spring 2024, Spain, Ireland, Norway, and Slovenia officially recognized the State of Palestine, elevating global diplomatic recognition above 145 countries. Prime Minister Mohammad Mustafa enacted public sector anti-corruption and fiscal transparency measures to prepare for unified governance across the West Bank and Gaza Strip.
