history: Inhabited by Maya, Lenca, and Tolupan peoples. Copán flourished as a major classic Maya center known for exquisite hieroglyphic stairways and carved stelae. Conquered by Spain in the 1520s, with indigenous Lenca chief Lempira leading heroic resistance. Gained independence in 1821 from Spain. Francisco Morazán led the Federal Republic of Central America in the 1830s. The early 20th century was dominated by US banana multinationals (United Fruit, Standard Fruit). Survived 1969 Football War with El Salvador; returned to constitutional civilian democracy in 1982.
recentEvents2020_2026: President Xiomara Castro assumed presidency in 2022; concluded major trade and investment agreements with China; expanded Palmerola International Airport.

Watershed protection

history: Inhabited by the Taíno who named the island Xaymaca ('Land of Wood and Water'). Columbus arrived in 1494. Spanish rule ceded to Britain in 1655 under Oliver Cromwell's forces. Sugar plantations powered by enslaved Africans made Jamaica Britain's most valuable colony. Escaped Africans formed independent Maroon communities in the Cockpit Country, waging successful guerrilla wars against the British to secure autonomy in the 1739 treaty under Queen Nanny. Sam Sharpe led the 1831 Baptist War that accelerated British abolition of slavery in 1834. Achieved independence on August 6, 1962 under Sir Alexander Bustamante.
recentEvents2020_2026: Achieved historic economic debt-to-GDP reduction below 75%; reached record-breaking tourism arrivals exceeding 4.3 million visitors; advanced parliamentary constitutional commission on republican transition.
historicalFigures: Queen Nanny of the Maroons (National Hero)
Marcus Garvey (Pan-African leader and National Hero)

education: University of the West Indies (UWI) Mona Campus (founding campus, premier research center in the Caribbean) and University of Technology (UTech).
healthcare: University Hospital of the West Indies and Kingston Public Hospital provide major regional medical care.

history: Cradle of monumental Mesoamerican civilizations: Olmec ('mother culture'), Teotihuacan, Maya, Toltec, Zapotec, and the Aztec Empire (Tenochtitlan, founded 1325). Hernán Cortés led the Spanish conquest in 1521, establishing the Viceroyalty of New Spain. Father Miguel Hidalgo launched the War of Independence with the Grito de Dolores on September 16, 1810; independence achieved in 1821. Benito Juárez defended the republic and defeated French intervention in the 1860s. The Mexican Revolution (1910–1920) led by Francisco Madero, Emiliano Zapata, and Pancho Villa established modern social rights and land reform.
recentEvents2020_2026: Elected Dr. Claudia Sheinbaum as the first female president in Mexican history in June 2024; completed the Maya Train (Tren Maya) circling the Yucatán Peninsula and the Interoceanic Corridor of the Isthmus of Tehuantepec; capitalized on massive nearshoring manufacturing investments.

ethnicGroups: Indigenous ~21.5% (identifying as indigenous by culture and language)

The 20th century was shaped by Augusto C. Sandino's resistance against US occupation, followed by the Somoza dynasty dictatorship (1936–1979). The Sandinista Revolution overthrew Somoza in 1979, leading to the Contra War in the 1980s until democratic elections in 1990.

history: Inhabited by indigenous Cuevas, Guna, and Chibcha peoples. Vasco Núñez de Balboa crossed the Isthmus in 1513, becoming the first European to sight the Pacific Ocean. Panama became the Spanish Empire's royal transshipment hub for Peruvian silver (Camino Real). Gained independence from Spain in 1821 and joined Gran Colombia. In 1903, backed by the United States, Panama separated from Colombia to build the Panama Canal, opened in August 1914. The Torrijos-Carter Treaties (1977) transferred full sovereignty of the Canal and the Canal Zone to Panama on December 31, 1999. In 2016, completed the historic $5.4B Panama Canal Expansion.
recentEvents2020_2026: Elected José Raúl Mulino as president in May 2024; executed multi-billion-dollar water-saving initiatives ensuring full vessel transits through the Panama Canal; opened Panama Metro Line 3 connecting western suburbs.

Gained independence on August 31, 1962 under Dr. Eric Williams (celebrated historian and founding prime minister), and became a republic in 1976.

Devastated by the War of the Triple Alliance (1864–1870 against Brazil, Argentina, Uruguay), losing over half its population, followed by victory in the Chaco War (1932–1935). The 20th century was defined by massive oil discoveries around Lake Maracaibo. Hugo Chávez was elected in 1998, initiating the 'Bolivarian Revolution'.

history: Inhabited continuously for over 65,000 years by Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples, representing the oldest surviving living cultures on Earth. European charted visits in the 17th century culminated in Captain James Cook claiming the east coast for Britain in 1770. First Fleet established penal colony at Sydney Cove in 1788. Six British colonies federated into the Commonwealth of Australia in 1901. ANZAC legend forged in WWI at Gallipoli. Post-WWII mass immigration transformed Australia into one of the world's most successful multicultural nations.
recentEvents2020_2026: Accelerated renewable energy rollout to reach 82% clean grid target; implemented AUKUS Pillar 1 and 2 security framework; co-hosted FIFA Women's World Cup 2023 with record global viewership; approved major indigenous sea country protections.

nationalIdentity: Defined by First Nations deep heritage, egalitarian outdoor lifestyle, sporting obsession, and cosmopolitan multicultural vibrancy.

Gained independence in 1970. Navigated several military coups before establishing the 2013 constitution guaranteeing equal citizenship.

name: Kiribati
motto: Te Mauri, Te Raoi ao Te Tabomoa (Health, Peace and Prosperity)
highestPoint: Unnamed point on Banaba Island (81 m)
longestRiver: None (atoll geography)
climate: Tropical maritime; warm and humid moderated by trade winds; periodic droughts
naturalHazards: Sea-level rise and coastal flooding
King tides inundating low atolls
Freshwater lens salinization
environmentalIssues: Vulnerability to climate change
Severe freshwater scarcity
Overcrowding in South Tarawa
biodiversity: Phoenix Islands Protected Area (one of Earth's largest marine protected areas, vital coral and seabird sanctuary)
timeZone: UTC+12:00 (Gilbert Islands), UTC+13:00 (Phoenix Islands), UTC+14:00 (Line Islands - first to see the sunrise)
legislature: Maneaba ni Maungatabu (House of Assembly)
latestElections: Parliamentary and presidential elections August–October 2024
politicalSituation: President Taneti Maamau re-elected in late 2024; strategic focus on national climate resilience, coastal sea wall fortification, and sustainable tuna fisheries.
foreignRelations: Member of UN, Pacific Islands Forum, Commonwealth; global leader in raising climate change awareness.
military: No standing military; police service (Kiribati Police) with maritime surveillance patrol boat.

history: Inhabited for millennia by Micronesian seafarers who mastered open-ocean outrigger voyaging. Explored by Captain Thomas Gilbert in 1788, giving rise to the name 'Gilbert Islands'. Became a British protectorate in 1892 and joined with the Ellice Islands (Tuvalu) as the Gilbert and Ellice Islands Colony in 1916. Scene of the intense WWII Battle of Tarawa in 1943. Gained independence in 1979 under the name Kiribati. In 1995, realigned the International Date Line so all its territory shares the same calendar day.
recentEvents2020_2026: Re-elected President Maamau in late 2024; completed major climate resilience coastal defenses on South Tarawa; implemented sustainable fisheries licensing under the Parties to the Nauru Agreement (PNA).
education: Kiribati Teachers College and USP Kiribati Campus; compulsory primary and junior secondary education.
healthcare: Tungaru Central Hospital in Nawerewere provides main medical services alongside island dispensaries.
socialCustoms: Centering communal life around the Maneaba (sacred village meeting house), respect for unimwane (elders), sharing of catches.
etiquette: Remove shoes before entering a Maneaba or home, bow slightly when passing seated elders, accept offered refreshments.
nationalIdentity: Defined by incredible ocean voyaging heritage, tight-knit communal Maneaba culture, and resolute climate survival advocacy.
industries: Commercial tuna fishing license revenues
Copra processing
Handicrafts and seaweed harvesting
naturalResources: Vast exclusive economic zone (3.5 million km² rich in tuna)
energy: Expanding solar mini-grids on outer islands, diesel generation in South Tarawa
tourism: Renowned world destination for bonefishing and seabird watching on Kiritimati (Christmas Island), and WWII historical tours on Betio.
employment: Major employment in public administration, commercial seafaring on international merchant ships, and subsistence fishing.
debtInflation: Fiscal stability anchored by the Revenue Equalization Reserve Fund (RERF) sovereign wealth fund and sustainable fishing revenue.
transport: South Tarawa causeways linking atoll islets; domestic passenger ships connecting outer islands.
ports: Port of Betio (main international container and fishing dock)
cuisine: Fresh tuna sashimi, Raw fish in coconut cream, Roasted breadfruit, Babai (giant swamp taro), Kamaimai (sweet boiled coconut syrup).
music: Polyphonic choral chants, harmonious body clapping, rhythmic singing in the Maneaba.
dance: Famous standing and seated bird-mimicking dances with swift head movements mimicking the frigatebird.
art: Woven pandanus sleeping mats, shark-tooth swords (historical armor), cowrie shell necklaces.

literature: Oral genealogies and sailing chants passed down across generations; poetry by Teweiariki Teaero.
cinema: Documentaries on climate resilience including Anote's Ark (Sundance Film Festival).
sports: Weightlifting (David Katoatau - Commonwealth Games gold medalist), Football, Traditional wrestling.
media: Te Uekera, Kiribati Newstar, Radio Kiribati (BPA).

worldHeritageSites: Phoenix Islands Protected Area (PIPA - one of the world's largest marine protected areas)
unescoIntangible: Traditional Maneaba governance and building knowledge

history: Inhabited for over 3,000 years by seafaring Austronesian peoples. On Pohnpei, the legendary Saudeleur Dynasty built the monumental megalithic stone city of Nan Madol (often called the 'Venice of the Pacific') between 1200 and 1500 CE. Yap developed the famous Rai stone money trade. Colonized by Spain, sold to Germany in 1899, captured by Japan in 1914, and administered by the US after WWII under the UN Trust Territory of the Pacific Islands. Federated into an independent constitutional republic in 1979 and entered free association with the US in 1986.
recentEvents2020_2026: Concluded the renewed 20-year Compact of Free Association with Washington securing vital infrastructure funding; advanced conservation around Nan Madol; hosted Pacific regional environmental congresses.

Discovery of immense high-grade phosphate rock deposits in 1900 transformed the island into a major mining center. Administered after WWI by Australia, the UK, and New Zealand under a League of Nations mandate; occupied by Japan during WWII. Gained independence in 1968, becoming the world's smallest independent republic. Phosphate revenues made Nauru one of the world's richest countries per capita in the 1970s before deposits were depleted.

Dutchman Abel Tasman sighted the islands in 1642; Captain James Cook mapped the coastlines in 1769. The Treaty of Waitangi was signed on February 6, 1840, establishing British sovereignty while recognizing Māori land and chieftain rights. In 1893, New Zealand became the first self-governing country in the world to grant all women the right to vote. Gallipoli campaign in WWI solidified national identity alongside Australia. Today recognized as a model inclusive democracy.

Northern New Guinea became a German colony (Kaiser-Wilhelmsland) in 1884; southern Papua became British, transferred to Australia in 1902. Intense combat occurred during WWII along the Kokoda Track in 1942, where Australian and Papuan troops halted Japanese advances toward Port Moresby. Gained peaceful independence from Australia on September 16, 1975 under Grand Chief Sir Michael Somare.

The non-violent Mau movement resisted colonial rule under the slogan 'Samoa mo Samoa' (Samoa for Samoans). Gained independence on January 1, 1962, becoming the first Polynesian nation to reclaim sovereignty in the 20th century.

Tonga maintained its sovereignty throughout the colonial era under a Treaty of Friendship with Great Britain, remaining the only sovereign Polynesian kingdom.
recentEvents2020_2026: Rebuilt critical maritime and digital communication links after the historic January 2022 submarine eruption of Hunga Tonga–Hunga Ha'apai; welcomed global scientific missions studying the atmospheric plume; celebrated 150 years of the Tongan Constitution.

politicalSituation: Prime Minister Feleti Teo assumed office in February 2024; ratification of the historic Falepili Union treaty with Australia providing climate mobility and security guarantees.
foreignRelations: Member of UN, Commonwealth, Pacific Islands Forum; maintains formal diplomatic ties with the Republic of China (Taiwan); Falepili Union partnership with Australia.
military: No armed forces; small Tuvalu Police Service with maritime surveillance patrol boat HMTSS Te Mataili II.
adminDivisions: 9 island councils (representing the 9 atolls)
history: Inhabited for over 2,000 years by Polynesian voyagers predominantly from Samoa and Tonga. Explored by Spanish navigator Álvaro de Mendaña in 1568; named the 'Ellice Islands' in 1819. Became a British protectorate in 1892, amalgamated into the Gilbert and Ellice Islands Colony in 1916. Funafuti served as a major Allied airfield during WWII. In 1974, the Polynesian Ellice Islanders voted overwhelmingly to separate from the Micronesian Gilbertese (Kiribati). Gained independence on October 1, 1978 under the name Tuvalu ('Eight Standing Together').
recentEvents2020_2026: Signed and ratified the landmark Falepili Union with Australia offering annual climate residency pathways for Tuvaluans while guaranteeing security; completed Funafuti Coastal Adaptation reclamation raising land 1.5m above sea level; elected Feleti Teo Prime Minister in early 2024.
religions: Church of Tuvalu (Ekalesia Kelisiano Tuvalu - Calvinist Congregationalist) ~97%
education: University of the South Pacific (USP) Tuvalu Campus; Motufoua Secondary School on Vaitupu; compulsory primary schooling.
healthcare: Princess Margaret Hospital in Funafuti provides the nation's primary medical care; emergency evacuations referred to Fiji or New Zealand.
socialCustoms: Fatele dancing in the Maneapa (community meeting hall), communal sharing of fish catches (Inati), respect for village elders (Kaupule).

history: Inhabited for over 3,300 years by Lapita and Melanesian voyagers. Explored by Portuguese navigator Pedro Fernandes de Queirós in 1606, who thought he found the Great Southern Continent and named it 'Austrialia del Espiritu Santo'. Captain James Cook charted the islands in 1774, naming them the 'New Hebrides'. From 1906 until 1980, the islands were governed under a bizarre unique joint colonial administration known as the British-French Condominium (or 'Pandemonium'). During WWII, Espiritu Santo served as a massive Allied base (inspiring James Michener's Tales of the South Pacific). Gained independence on July 30, 1980 as the Republic of Vanuatu.
recentEvents2020_2026: Spearheaded the unanimous UN General Assembly resolution requesting an International Court of Justice (ICJ) advisory opinion on state climate responsibilities; rebuilt infrastructure following twin cyclones in 2023; expanded solar energy mini-grids.
historicalFigures: Father Walter Lini (Father of Independence and pioneer of Melanesian Socialism)
